#10005. Building AI factories at enterprise scale

SPONSORED FEATURE: ASUS wants to scale AI everywhere in the enterprise

AI has become a juggernaut, driving technical strategy in the tech sector and outside of it. With the worldwide server market growing 30 percent in a single year to hit $122.6bn in the first quarter of 2025, IDC now feels safe recategorizing AI-driven investment "from cyclical to durable".

The analyst company expects inference to account for over 70 percent of computing demand by next year, adding that it's growing fastest at the edge.

All this investment in AI infrastructure might once have come mainly for hyperscalers, but that's changing quickly. Adoption is spreading quickly beyond public cloud service providers into enterprise environments, IDC adds. They're eager to run agentic AI in-house.

There are plenty of reasons for companies to own their own AI infrastructure rather than offloading it to the cloud. One of these is data control, especially in regulated sectors such as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and the public sector that have sovereign data requirements. Another revolves around the need for predictable costing from tokens delivered on tunable in-house systems.

So what should companies look for in a supplier? Delivery speed will be a powerful driver for many who are under the gun to deliver AI initiatives for the business, especially during periods of constrained memory and CPU supply. Life cycle services will also come near the top of the list, for companies that need help managing everything from the power through to the reasoning LLM models and the workloads that use them. That need for expertise is unlikely to stop; companies will undergo changes in AI strategy as they get to grips with a still-evolving technology.

ASUS expects this AI surge to continue in the datacenter, but elsewhere too, specifically in edge locations (especially industrial use cases) and at developers' desks, as the applications that will power the enterprise get made. It wants to be top of peoples' list for hardware and services at all these places along the AI continuum.

At NVIDIA's GTC show in Berlin on Oct 21-22, it announced a full-stack AI offering that it's calling its Enterprise Agentic AI Solution. It's  three-layer affair, featuring:

ASUS AI Server and Infrastructure: Its selection of AI servers, including several new units.

ASUS AI Software Stack: Its software for integrating and controlling AI workflows.

ASUS AI HUB: A services operation that ties it all together.

These bring together some existing assets that ASUS had for enterprise AI users, along with some new ones. The time is right for an end-to-end offering with new hardware because of the way the market is shifting, say ASUS execs.

"ASUS servers help enterprises build high-performance agentic AI infrastructure capable of supporting both complex task execution and large-scale AI agent deployment, accelerating enterprise adoption of agentic AI," says Paul Ju, senior vice president and head of infrastructure solution BG at ASUS.

While generative AI initially spiked demand, the advent of agentic AI has sent compute demand into overdrive. Ju explains that the focus is expanding from the GPU.

"Historically, AI servers have been optimized primarily around GPU compute. But as enterprise AI shifts toward agentic AI, workloads increasingly revolve around a continuous ‘agent loop’ that is heavily CPU-dependent," he says. That loop takes in task planning, code execution, external tool invocation, and reflection or correction work.

The CPU's increased role in this execution work is creating bottlenecks in conventional AI servers, he adds.

The first such sticking point is single-thread performance, which leaves GPUs idling while they wait for CPUs to complete. The second lies in memory bandwidth. When this is managed on a per-core basis, it can slow things down when many agents run at once.

The multi-die design of many CPUs also penalizes them in AI environments, because accessing data across dies introduces latency, Ju argues. CPUs with cores and cache on different dies suffer latency when data has to cross between them. Maintaining cache coherency exacerbates that problem.

Finally, there's a security risk: a lack of hardware level sandbox isolation on some CPUs make it possible for prompt injection to reach core systems, he warns.

Customers also bring their own challenges as they grapple with different applications for AI. Enterprises evaluating AI server options have to match their server platforms to the projected AI workload profiles, Ju adds. Training a supervised learning model to batch-classify insurance claims takes different technical resources to running a low-latency reasoning employee chatbot.

ASUS wants to help customers solve problems like these wherever they come up. With this in mind, the company had plenty of goodies for onlookers at GTC.

Starting at the datacenter, the company announced both single and full-rack systems built around the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 eight-GPU server board. It has a 3U hybrid-cooled system, the XA NR11-E12L, along with the 2U 100 percent liquid-cooled XA NR11-E12, both targeting large AI reasoning workloads.

The two Rubin units target different use cases. The 3U hybrid liquid cooling system uses direct-to-chip liquid cooling on the 8GPU baseboard, along with air-cooled dual Xeon 6 chips on a sled. The company pegs this as the easy transition path into AI factory hardware. The 2U unit, with its 100 percent liquid cooling, is tailored for maximum PUE and compute density. It also uses a cable-free board-to-board design to keep its footprint low.

The kit will be speedy, too, with NVIDIA HGX Rubin offering 800Gbit of integrated bandwidth per GPU.

ASUS is promoting the serviceability of these units through their use of tool list CPU and GPU sleds. It claims up to a 50 percent time saving on maintenance operations for these units, meaning less downtime per service and ultimately a lower total cost of ownership.

ASUS is structuring its hardware proposition around speedy delivery so that customers can get hardware up and running to support their AI initiatives. That speed comes from validation carried out before delivery with the help of a pre-validated rack reference architecture.

In keeping with its focus on multiple designs for the right AI workload, ASUS also supports NVIDIA's modular MGX Blueprint for server builds. The selling point here is flexibility with a mixture of GPUs, CPUs, and networking options for enterprise inference, agents, and visual computing. This is the modular route for workloads that don't need the power of an 8-GPU HGX baseboard, and it covers a large gamut of enterprise inference and agentic use cases.

ASUS showcased MGX servers including the 6U XA P8A-E14AXL with its eight liquid-cooled NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. A 2U sibling, the XA P4N-E2, sports NVIDIA Vera processors for agentic work.

The ASUS booth also featured the ExpertCenter Pro ET900N G3, powered by the GB300 Grace Blackwell Superchip developer desktop with 748GB of coherent memory, and the Ascent GX10 based on NVIDIA DGX Spark  for agentic work. Also on show were the ProArt GR1X Mini PC and ProArt P16  and P14 laptop - the first laptops powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark - aimed at both developers and creators.

For edge installations, it showed the PE3000N, its rugged NVIDIA Jetson T5000-based edge-AI computer aimed at use cases including industrial environments. Announced a year ago, this delivers up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS of peak AI performance with 128GB of memory. Targeted at industrial AI environments was the PE6000G, a workstation-grade AI and simulation platform.

Equipment only supports an AI factory when there is power to run it. ASUS has been taking steps with NVIDIA as a partner here, adopting its DSX AI Factory platform with digital twin system for laying out hardware and power in AI factory environments. DSX supports equipment using the NVIDIA Vera Rubin processor line, which supports dry coolers and a lower PUE with a 45 degree centigrade warm water inlet.

ASUS configured racks become simulation-ready assets inside DSX, adopting its OpenUSD shared file format. That covers engineering data alongside the geometry for measuring real power draw and cooling requirements.

ASUS wanted to target cooling as part of the original design plan for the AI Factory, not as a facility afterthought. So, the DSX partnership allows implementation teams to model water temperature, flow, pressure, CDU placement, and piping within the digital twin model. They translate information from the planning resources that go around this, such as the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint framework, using the ASUS Infrastructure Deployment Center.

The digital twin system isn't just for design and setup. It's supposed to keep working after go-live so that AI factory operators can simulate changes before touching hardware. The ASUS Control Center monitors the infrastructure while DSX exchange links IT and operational technology data. Operators can validate changes in the simulation before flipping the switch to go live.

ASUS' goal here is clear: to assist enterprise customers as they tackle in-house AI opportunities while acknowledging that the performance profile and physical locations of their workloads will vary. As companies continue to evolve their understanding of AI and where it fits within the organization, they will need to be agile in how they plan and nurture their infrastructure from the datacenter out to the edge, and to the developer's desk.

The Berlin announcements tie it together in a neat package for organizations that need help with their agentic aspirations.

#10003. A new Go API for JSON

Stories about how and why companies use Go

How Go can help keep you secure by default

A complete introduction to building software with Go

Reference documentation for Go's standard library

Tips for writing clear, performant, and idiomatic Go code

Learn and network with Go developers from around the world

Michael Pratt, Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, and Damien Neil 4 November 2026

JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!

Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception. Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.

After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27! This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment, describing the problems with encoding/json and introducing the new packages.

Overall, encoding/json has held up well. The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible. However, in the years since its introduction, various users have identified numerous shortcomings.

There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json:

Imprecise handling of JSON syntax: Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value.

encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8, whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8. The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8, instead of introducing silent data corruption, which may cause problems downstream.

encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names. RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names, so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value, merge the values, discard the values, or report an error. The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value without a universally agreed upon meaning. This could be exploited by attackers in security applications and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635). The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.

Leaking nilness of slices and maps: JSON is often used to communicate with programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object. Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null, this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations. A survey indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default.

Case-insensitive unmarshaling: When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation.

Inconsistent calling of methods: Due to an implementation detail, MarshalJSON methods declared on a pointer receiver are inconsistently called by encoding/json. While regarded as a bug, this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior.

The API of encoding/json can be tricky or restrictive:

It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an io.Reader. Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v), which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input.

Options can be set on the Encoder and Decoder types, but cannot be used with the Marshal and Unmarshal functions. Similarly, types implementing the Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack. For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect when calling a custom UnmarshalJSON method.

The Compact, Indent, and HTMLEscape functions write to a bytes.Buffer instead of something more flexible like a []byte or io.Writer. This limits the usability of those functions.

Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations:

MarshalJSON: The MarshalJSON interface method forces the implementation to allocate the returned []byte. Also, the semantics require that encoding/json verify that the result is valid JSON and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation.

UnmarshalJSON: The UnmarshalJSON interface method requires that a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data). This forces encoding/json to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call UnmarshalJSON. Afterwards, the UnmarshalJSON method itself must parse the provided JSON value again.

Lack of streaming: Even though the Encoder and Decoder types operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader, they buffer the entire JSON value in memory. The Decoder.Token method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens.

Furthermore, if the implementation of a MarshalJSON or UnmarshalJSON method recursively calls the Marshal or Unmarshal function, then the performance becomes quadratic.

Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package.

While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise.

We could in principle declare separate names, such as MarshalV2 or UnmarshalV2, but that is tantamount to creating a parallel namespace within the same package. This leads us to encoding/json/v2 (henceforth called v2), where we can make these changes within a separate v2 namespace in contrast to encoding/json (henceforth called v1).

Before discussing the v2 API, we first introduce the encoding/json/jsontext package that lays the foundation for improvements to JSON in Go.

JSON serialization in Go can be broken down into two primary components:

We use the terms “encode” and “decode” to describe syntactic functionality and the terms “marshal” and “unmarshal” to describe semantic functionality. We aim to provide a clear distinction between functionality that is purely concerned with encoding versus that of marshaling.

This diagram provides an overview of this separation. Purple blocks represent types, while blue blocks represent functions or methods. The direction of the arrows approximately represents the flow of data. The bottom half of the diagram, implemented by the jsontext package, contains functionality that is only concerned with syntax, while the upper half, implemented by the json/v2 package, contains functionality that assigns semantic meaning to syntactic data handled by the bottom half.

The basic API of jsontext is the following:

The jsontext package provides functionality for interacting with JSON at a syntactic level and derives its name from RFC 8259, section 2 where the grammar for JSON data is literally called JSON-text. Since it only interacts with JSON at a syntactic level, it does not depend on Go reflection.

The Encoder and Decoder provide support for encoding and decoding JSON values and tokens. The constructors accept variadic options that affect the particular behavior of encoding and decoding. Unlike the Encoder and Decoder types declared in v1, the new types in jsontext avoid muddling the distinction between syntax and semantics and operate in a truly streaming manner.

A JSON value is a complete unit of data and is represented in Go as a named []byte. It is identical to RawMessage in v1, which is now a type alias to jsontext.Value. A JSON value is syntactically composed of one or more JSON tokens. A JSON token is represented in Go as the opaque Token type with constructors and accessor methods. It is analogous to Token in v1 but is designed to represent arbitrary JSON tokens without allocation.

To resolve the fundamental performance problems with the MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON interface methods, we need an efficient way of encoding and decoding JSON as a streaming sequence of tokens and values. In v2, we introduce the MarshalJSONTo and UnmarshalJSONFrom interface methods that operate on an Encoder or Decoder, allowing the methods’ implementations to process JSON in a purely streaming manner. Thus, the json package need not be responsible for validating or formatting a JSON value returned by MarshalJSON, nor would it need to be responsible for determining the boundaries of a JSON value provided to UnmarshalJSON. These responsibilities belong to the Encoder and Decoder.

Building on the jsontext package, we now introduce the encoding/json/v2 package. It is designed to fix the problems in v1, while remaining familiar to users of the v1 package. Our goal is that usages of v1 will operate mostly the same if directly migrated to v2.

Here, we primarily cover the high-level API of v2. For examples on how to use it, we encourage readers to study the examples in the v2 package, the “Working with JSON” tutorial, or read Anton Zhiyanov’s blog covering the topic.

The Marshal and Unmarshal functions have a signature similar to v1, but accept options to configure their behavior. The MarshalWrite and UnmarshalRead functions directly operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader, avoiding the need to temporarily construct an Encoder or Decoder just to write or read from such types. The MarshalEncode and UnmarshalDecode functions operate on a jsontext.Encoder and jsontext.Decoder and are actually the underlying implementation of the previously mentioned functions. Unlike v1, options are a first-class argument to each of the marshal and unmarshal functions, greatly extending the flexibility and configurability of v2. There are several options available in v2 which are not covered by this article.

Similar to v1, v2 allows types to define their own JSON representation by satisfying particular interfaces.

The Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces are identical to those in v1. The new MarshalerTo and UnmarshalerFrom interfaces allow a type to represent itself as JSON using a jsontext.Encoder or jsontext.Decoder. This allows options to be forwarded down the call stack, since options can be retrieved via the Options accessor method on the Encoder or Decoder.

See the OrderedObject example for how to implement a custom type that maintains the ordering of JSON object members.

In v2, the caller of Marshal and Unmarshal can also specify a custom JSON representation for any arbitrary type, where caller-specified functions take precedence over type-defined methods or the default representation for a particular type.

MarshalFunc and MarshalToFunc construct a custom marshaler that can be passed to a Marshal call using WithMarshalers to override the marshaling of particular types. Similarly, UnmarshalFunc and UnmarshalFromFunc support similar customization for Unmarshal.

The ProtoJSON example demonstrates how this feature allows serialization of all proto.Message types to be handled by the protojson package.

While v2 aims to behave mostly the same as v1, its behavior has changed in some ways to address problems in v1, most notably:

v2 reports an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8.

v2 reports an error if a JSON object contains a duplicate name.

v2 marshals a nil Go slice or Go map as an empty JSON array or JSON object, respectively.

v2 unmarshals a JSON object into a Go struct using a case-sensitive match from the JSON member name to the Go field name.

v2 redefines the omitempty tag option to omit a field if it would have encoded as an “empty” JSON value (which are null, "", [], and {}).

v2 reports an error when trying to serialize a time.Duration, which currently has no default representation, but provides options to let the caller decide.

For most behavior changes, there is a struct tag option or caller-specified option that can configure the behavior to operate under v1 or v2 semantics, or even other caller-determined behavior. See “Migrating to v2” for more information.

The Marshal performance of v2 is roughly at parity with v1. Sometimes it is slightly faster, but other times it is slightly slower. The Unmarshal performance of v2 is significantly faster than v1, with benchmarks demonstrating improvements of up to 10x.

In order to obtain greater performance gains, existing implementations of Marshaler and Unmarshaler should migrate to also implement MarshalerTo and UnmarshalerFrom, so that they can benefit from processing JSON in a purely streaming manner. For example, recursive parsing of OpenAPI specifications in UnmarshalJSON methods significantly hurt performance in a particular service of Kubernetes (see kubernetes/kube-openapi#315), while switching to UnmarshalJSONFrom improved performance by orders of magnitude.

For more benchmark details, see the go-json-experiment/jsonbench repository.

On top of structural improvements, we’re continuing to invest in performance optimizations in the implementation for cases where the v2 implementation is slower than v1. You can expect additional improvements in Go 1.28.

The Go 1 compatibility promise is a core guarantee from the Go project that allows developers to build applications that will stand the test of time and continue working on future versions of Go.

The original encoding/json and new encoding/json/v2 packages are of course both subject to the Go 1 compatibility promise. Applications using v1 will continue to be supported indefinitely and need not ever migrate to v2.

That said, when designing the v2 packages we wanted to do better than keeping v1 supported. We wanted to ensure that v1 and v2 are compatible with one another so that packages using different versions can work together. Doing so allows a smooth ecosystem migration rather than forcing users to use one version or another due to the choices of their dependencies.

For instance, suppose your package uses v2 to marshal a struct containing a field with a type defined in another package. That package may use the original v1 MarshalJSON method to define its marshaling behavior. No problem, v2 supports MarshalJSON methods, so marshaling will continue working as expected.

Vice versa, suppose your package uses v1 to marshal the same struct. The other package may use the v2 MarshalJSONTo method for better performance. No problem here either, as the v1 implementation supports v2’s MarshalJSONTo method under the hood.

We’ve achieved this by designing the new packages such that, under the hood, v1 is implemented in terms of v2. As mentioned above, v2 supports a variety of Options. Each behavior difference is controlled by one of these options. Thus, v1 can be implemented in terms of v2 by passing the full set of v1 compatibility options.

With this approach, backwards-compatible additions such as new methods (e.g., MarshalJSONTo) or new struct tags (e.g., embed) are automatically supported to the benefit of existing v1 users.

Implementing v1 in terms of v2 options has the additional benefit of allowing gradual migration of callsites.

encoding/json documents the full set of behavior differences between v1 and v2, and which option controls those behaviors.

Many applications can migrate directly to v2 with no visible behavior changes, but applications that depend on v1 behavior can use the options to change only the behaviors they depend on.

For example, we can select all v2 behavior except that duplicate names are allowed:

Alternatively, we can select all v1 behavior except that duplicate names are disallowed:

The encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide goes into more detail, covering a variety of scenarios for approaching migration of an application from v1 to v2.

For additional references on working with the new JSON packages, see:

The planning for a new major version of encoding/json spanned years. In late 2020, spurred on by the inability to fix issues in the current package, Daniel Martí (one of the maintainers of encoding/json) first drafted his thoughts on what a hypothetical v2 package should look like. Separately, after previous work on the Go API for Protocol Buffers, Joe Tsai was disappointed that the protojson package needed to use a custom JSON implementation because encoding/json was neither capable of adhering to the stricter JSON standard that the Protocol Buffer specification required, nor of efficiently serializing JSON in a streaming manner.

Believing a brighter future for JSON was both beneficial and achievable, Daniel and Joe joined forces to brainstorm on v2 and started to build a prototype (with the initial code being a polished version of the JSON serialization logic from the Go protobuf module). Over time, a few others (Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Damien Neil, Austin Clements, and Michael Pratt) joined the effort by providing design review, code review, and regression testing. Many of the early discussions are publicly available in our recorded meetings and meeting notes. Later discussions are available in our encoding/json/v2 working group meeting notes.

This work has been public since the beginning, and we increasingly involved the wider Go community, first with a GopherCon talk and discussion posted in late 2023, formal proposal posted in early 2025, and finally adopting encoding/json/v2 as a Go experiment in Go 1.25 for wider-scale testing by all Go users.

The v2 effort took about 6 years to reach this point, incorporating feedback from many contributors and also gaining valuable empirical experience from use in production settings.

It’s worth noting that it’s largely been developed and promoted by people not employed by Google, demonstrating that the Go project is a collaborative endeavor with a thriving global community dedicated to improving the Go ecosystem.

#10002. Meta brings Conductor on board its model train

Agent orchestration startup gets its exit

Meta has acquired AI coding startup Conductor, signaling interest in applying AI to software engineering tasks.

Charlie Holtz, the startup's co-founder and CEO, made the announcement in a blog post. He also revealed that the company's hosted Conductor Cloud, a sandbox for hosted agents, will go read-only on November 13 and shut down on November 20.

Conductor, the eponymous company's macOS app for running multiple coding agents simultaneously in isolated copies of Git projects, will continue working for the next few months, and the biz expects to provide a way to transfer Conductor Cloud workspaces to local machines.

But in early 2027, Conductor will no longer receive new models or critical bug fixes.

A Meta spokesperson confirmed that the acquisition will strengthen the company's developer-oriented AI capabilities but declined to elaborate further. Perhaps Conductor will play nicely with Muse Code, Meta's recently introduced coding agent.

Having spent heavily on strengthening its AI research lab, Meta has moderated its appetite for big acquisitions since April when China blocked its $2 billion offer for Manus AI, a developer of software agents.

Meta's other acquisitions this year, Moltbook, Assured Robot Intelligence, and Stilla, are also AI-oriented but more modest in scope.

The Conductor deal comes without an announced price, and follows in the footsteps of Meta regaining credibility as a model provider: Llama 4 disappointed but Meta's recent Muse Wonder and Spark models rank respectably among the top LLMs at the moment.

In Meta's most recent conference call for investors [PDF], CEO Mark Zuckerberg said his company aims to provide AI agents that non-technical people can deploy for business tasks.

"What we see is a lot of people are actually using Muse today to help run especially small businesses," he said. "And we think that there's both an opportunity to help create an agent that people use to really enable them to automate and do a lot of the parts of spinning up a small business that are just kind of difficult and time-consuming but aren't the core thing that a person is trying to do."

Meta's AI strategy, as Zuckerberg describes it, is focused on collecting transaction fees from businesses for enabling agentic commerce, selling advanced AI capabilities to developers in the form of model access or tokens, charging for Muse to automate business tasks, and applying AI to personalize and improve results from ads.

It's a good time to run an AI-related startup, as leading model companies seek to add value beyond offering AI models. Models themselves have become commoditized to the point that only a few leading model makers can get away with charging a premium. In an effort to maintain that lead, top model makers have been purchasing innovation (and talent) while they are still flush with investor funds.

On Wednesday, OpenAI said it plans to acquire Pierre Computer Company, maker of distributed storage service Code Storage⁠ and open-source developer tools. And a few months earlier, the ChatGPT maker snapped up Ona, which makes cloud development environments for agents.

Anthropic's most recent developer tools deal involved Stainless back in May. Its purchase of Opaque Systems, which offers confidential computing technology, could also be squeezed into the developer tool category.

At some point, when it becomes clearer what kinds of AI services people will pay for, startup acquisitions may become more focused. But for the moment, with software development being the most successful use of AI, makers of AI-oriented developer tooling have a shot at a glorious exit. ®

#9998. Uber says it alone can make robotaxis pay, hours after Waymo quit its app

Google-owned autonomous cab company Waymo has revealed it will stop allowing Uber users to book its robo-cabs, hours before the OG rideshare giant made a case for all autonomous vehicle fleet operators to use its platform instead of creating their own.

This slow-motion fender bender played out across Wednesday, starting with Waymo Co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana telling Bloomberg that her company would end a partnership that saw it work exclusively with Uber in Austin and Atlanta.

Mawakana said Waymo wasn’t happy about the fact that when users of Uber’s app requested a ride in one of its robo-cabs, they weren’t guaranteed to get one.

News of that break-up came on the same day that Uber announced its quarterly results. As is common on such occasions, the company published remarks [PDF] its execs intend to make during an earnings call.

CEO Dara Khosrowshahi used those remarks to promote the idea that Uber is the natural home for robotaxi fleet operators, because it already delivers around 30 percent higher trips per vehicle per day compared to apps run by autonomous cab companies. He said that higher utilization rate, plus use of shared charging and maintenance infrastructure, can deliver “higher fleet profitability even after paying Uber’s marketplace fee.”

“As autonomous technology becomes more widely available, we believe this ability to commercialize vehicles profitably will become an increasingly important source of competitive advantage and value capture.”

The two events are deliciously ironic, because Uber is arguing the scale of its platform makes it the ideal host for third-party players – just as Google does with its search, app store, and YouTube services. Left unsaid is that the two companies hold concerningly dominant positions in their respective markets.

Khosrowshahi also outlined more ways Uber intends to strengthen its position, including by putting around 2,000 robo-cabs on the road in 2027, before “a much larger commercial ramp beginning in 2028.” That plan means Uber will run some cars itself and rely on third-party robo-cab operators who allow bookings on its app.

“Importantly, building a broad ecosystem does not mean spreading our resources evenly,” the CEO explained. “We intend to maintain an open platform while concentrating capital, integration resources, and hands-on deployment support behind a smaller group of partners with the clearest paths to commercial scale and attractive economics at maturity.”

Or in other words, as Uber uses more robo-cabs, it will try to maximize profits.

Uber users booked $59.8 billion worth of services in its third quarter, up 20 percent year-over-year. The company recognized $14.75 billion of that as revenue, a ten percent improvement.

Rideshare accounted for $29.5 billion of bookings and $7.5 billion of revenue. Delivery services brought in $5.5 billion of revenue on $28.5 billion of bookings.

No wonder Khosrowshahi wants more robo-cabs: they’ll boost Uber’s more lucrative business.

The company might need that boost because Australia’s High Court yesterday decided [PDF] that the company must pay AU$81 million ($57 million) in State payroll taxes because the fees paid to rideshare drivers are effectively wages. While the case considered Uber’s activities in one of Australia’s six States, all of them charge payroll tax. The case is one of many around the world in which courts have found gig workers should be treated as employees for legal and tax purposes. The High Court is Australia’s highest judicial authority and like-minded jurisdictions around the world are aware of its decisions, potentially making more trouble for Uber further down the road. ®

#9994. Can 23,000 quantum qubits break RSA-2048?

Another quantum computing company’s “Breaking X with N qubits in time T”:

Alice & Bob, a French QC company, claims (in a paper posted on cryptographers’ ePrint) that a quantum computer they may eventually build could, with just 22,593 qubits, break (factor) RSA-2048 in about 𝝅 ≈ 3.14 days. As an orange–pineapple comparison, Google’s OMG press release in March was about a system with half a million qubits, to break 256-bit ECDLP.

As usual, several people have asked me how scary this is—and as usual some of them have decided that it’s actually scary and expect my confirmation, and ask me for justification when I say it’s not, so this post is kinda serving this purpose.

The short answer: it’s interesting research, but we (well, A&B) are nowhere near having such a machine—and a lot of “ifs” are involved.

First, quick context: QCs use qubits instead of ordinary bits; a problem is that qubits are extremely fragile, errors happen frequently, they must be corrected, and correcting them requires… more qubits, running quantum error correction. That’s one of the main obstacles to building QCs.

A&B is developing a special type of qubit, which is a type of cat qubit (the “cat” is Schrödinger’s, a reference to the way cat qubits encode information). Cat qubits are designed to make certain errors rare. A&B built systems with up to 18 cat qubits.

The paper is essentially a thought experiment based on premise “Imagine we could build a large quantum computer using improved versions of our qubits, then how efficiently could it break RSA-2048?” It’s also sort a bit of a truism “If we could build what’s necessary to break RSA-2048, then guess what…”

A&B’s paper combines assumptions about future hardware with error correction techniques and an optimized implementation of Shor’s algorithms. Their calculations suggest that around 23,000 qubits would be sufficient.

Their main calculation assumes that a particular type of error (bit-flip) would occur, on average, only once every 100 years per qubit. That’s a pretty low error rate for a qubit, even for a cat one:

For comparison, A&B’s published experiments demonstrated this kind of error occurring, on average, once every few minutes (under certain conditions and much more frequently during some quantum operations.)

The paper acknowledges a gap of more than 100 million times between the assumed reliability and the experimental results it uses for comparison.

There’s also the scale detail: A&B has developed experimental systems with up to 18 qubits; they’d need another 22,575 qubits.

The paper mentions an alternative design with more realistic error rate assumptions, requiring around 45,000 qubits. But again thus depends on error-correction techniques that haven’t yet been demonstrated.

I feel like competition among QC companies is increasingly a competition for attention; it encourages them to publish scary-looking numbers based on more or less plausible assumptions. To be fair, A&B’s paper is transparent about its assumptions and is solid quantum engineering work. The problem is less the research itself than how its results are presented and promoted.

So the research isnt worthless: estimating the resources needed to break crypto is important and improvements to quantum algorithms and architectures deserve attention. But calculating what an hypothetical machine could do is different from demonstrating that we know how to build that machine.

That’s the distinction you must keep in mind when reading OMG-quantum headlines.

Oh and another result (claimed under similar assumptions) is an architecture to solve ECDLP in about one hour with ~30,000 qubits:

Thanks for such a thoughtful post and debunking the scary title of this paper. It’s annoying to me that companies keep on producing assumptions that are hard to parse without deep expertise so they can feed into the cycle of quantum hype and media and PR and panic and amplification. Wish research now focused on helping companies and other choose what to migrate and figure out cheap tooling to facilitate PQC

#9992. Microsoft admits certifications can be a drag, launches creds that recognize skills

‘Pro Badges’ don’t require a test, Microsoft awards them by watching you use GitHub

When The Register writes about professional certifications offered by vendors, we often receive comments arguing that such credentials are nowhere near as valuable as real-world experience. Now, Microsoft has acknowledged there’s some merit in that argument.

Redmond revealed its stance last week in a post from general manager for content and insights Cameron Percy, who  observed: “For years, people have asked for a simpler way to prove the skills they use in the flow of work, without stepping away to prepare for another test.”

Microsoft’s response is the “Pro Badge,” a new form of credential that Percy wrote “works alongside Microsoft Certifications.”

“Certifications show that you can solve problems in a role or field. Pro Badge shows how you use a specific product in your everyday work. Together, they give a more complete picture of what you can do.”

“Instead of capturing skills on a single test day, this approach keeps pace with your work and the products you use,” Percy added. “It gives you a current, verified signal of what you can do, at no cost and without a separate exam or study guide.”

The first Pro Badge is for GitHub Copilot. To earn it, users need only visit learn.github.com and sign in with their GitHub account.

Going through those steps fires up a “proficiency engine” that Microsoft says “gets to work analyzing relevant product usage signals and evaluating them against a defined proficiency framework.” Percy’s post says it “systematically uses evidence from everyday product use to calculate and automatically update your proficiency level.”

Microsoft offers five levels of proficiency: beginner, intermediate, proficient, advanced, and expert. To earn a Pro Badge, users must reach the proficient level.

A beginner has had “first contact” with GitHub and “understands what Copilot is, where it can be used, and how it might fit into everyday development workflows.”

An intermediate user is “familiar with web-based collaboration features, core IDE features, model management, agent configuration, customization options, and techniques for managing context.”

To score the Pro Badge, users will need to demonstrate “practical ability to work on projects” and use GitHub “across typical scenarios, demonstrated through consistent hands-on usage across multiple repositories and extended periods.”

“A Proficient user can use many web and IDE features, select appropriate models, and apply customizations to tailor Copilot for specific project needs. They have experimented with extended features and are aware of extensibility/integration options.”

At the time of writing, Redmond hasn’t defined expert or advanced proficiency. It has published more criteria for the first three levels here.

Microsoft has kindly integrated GitHub’s learning site with LinkedIn, which it owns, so users can add Pro Badges to their profiles.

Percy’s post suggests Microsoft has other Pro Badges in the works.

Elsewhere, Microsoft makes it plain that Pro Badges won’t replace its other credentials.

“GitHub Verified Proficiency is part of Microsoft Pro Badge, a new credential type designed to recognize skills as they are applied in the flow of work,” explains a page offering detail of the new cred. “It does not replace certifications or Microsoft Applied Skills. It adds a third signal: how skills show up through everyday product use.”

The Register welcomes comment on this new approach to professional credentials. ®

#9988. VMware quietly offers European users extended sales and support for low-end vSphere

Version 8 of Standard and Enterprise Plus will stay alive until October 2028

VMware appears to have made a concession to European regulators by extending the life of its low-end vSphere Standard and Enterprise Plus products.

The virtualization pioneer quietly announced the extension in the November 4 blog post in which it announced a new low-end product called vSphere Express, which The Register reported yesterday.

We based our report about vSphere Express on an interview, and on material provided by VMware – which sent a version of the blog post linked to above.

The version we saw did not include the following paragraph, the contents of which were not mentioned in our interview:

“Furthermore, for customers in countries in the European Economic Area, vSphere Standard version 8 and vSphere Enterprise Plus version 8 will remain available for sale until October 31, 2027, and will have Extended Support included in any active subscriptions to those offerings until the earlier of the applicable subscription end date or October 31, 2028.”

The latter date is more than a year past the October 11, 2027, end-of-general-support date for the more capable vSphere 8 and Cloud Foundation 5.x products.

“This has the potential to be a positive development for organisations within the European Economic Area,” independent analyst Michael Warrilow told The Register. “It could provide them up to an extra 12 months to transition vSphere 8 to VCF 9 and/or migrate workloads to another platform.”

Warrilow thinks European users should seek “absolute clarity” from VMware about the specifics of its offer.

“What level of extended support will be provided and what longer-term commitments will need to be made? I cannot find any of that detail,” he wrote.

A reminder: VMware has promised in the past to make patches available for users who choose to persist with perpetual licenses instead of moving to its preferred subscriptions. The Broadcom business unit later paused patch downloads for months, claiming it needed to adjust its website to make them possible.

Warrilow wonders why VMware will keep selling vSphere Standard only in Europe and suggested “regulatory muscle” is the reason.

Regulators around the world cleared Broadcom’s acquisition of VMware. In Europe, authorities have since revisited the matter.

Lobby group Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe (CISPE) has succeeded in having the European Commission open an antitrust investigation into whether VMware’s channel changes inappropriately shaped the cloud infrastructure provider market. The Register understands CISPE feels regulators are receptive to its arguments.

In the Netherlands, local courts enforced a VMware support contract of the sort that Broadcom has tried to walk away from at other users.

Warrilow wonders if VMware might now change its policy regarding vSphere Standard in other countries.

“The subsequent question is how can organisations in other regions get the same concessions from Broadcom? I would encourage them to amplify their voice by rallying industry associations and user groups to the cause whilst lobbying the regulators in their jurisdiction.”

Overall, however, he thinks VMware’s decision isn’t enormously impactful.

“Ultimately, all it does is buy a little more time to upgrade or migrate,” he wrote.

It may not even do that, as The Register often heard that VMware seldom issued quotes for vSphere Standard or Enterprise Plus.

Paul Turner, chief product officer for VMware’s Cloud Foundation Division, told The Register that inappropriate incentives for channel partners caused that situation, and that VMware later fixed it.

Continental users will be hoping VMware got that effort right. ®

#9983. When datacenters lose power, generators should kick in. That didn’t happen for Google in London

October outage caused by bad PLC config exposed at a time maintenance work reduced resilience

Google Cloud has revealed that the cause of the October 20 outage in its europe-west-2-b availability zone was a ‘misconfiguration’ of its systems that meant its emergency generators didn’t start.

The outage at the London facility caused service interruptions at outfits including Lloyds, HSBC, Royal Mail, and Revolut.

In a November 4 update to its service status  page, Google explained what went wrong.

“The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture — where the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load — backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC),” Google revealed.

The facility gets its juice from two independent utility feeders, which Google calls “A” and “B”. There’s also a “standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events.”

Google says the root cause of the incident was failure in an external underground cable through which its power supplier brings ‘leccy to its bit barns.

That cable connects to primary feeder A and it broke at a time when feeder B wasn’t working.

“Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026,” Google admitted. “Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while the feed B breaker remained in an open position to allow repairs to be conducted on the B feeder pathway.”

That shouldn’t be a problem for a top-tier operator like Google, which knows it needs to install backup sources of electricity like uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and on-site generators.

Indeed, europe-west-2-b employs UPSes that Google says can keep things up and running for five minutes if the availability zone loses its connection to the grid.

The UPSes worked, but a “voltage-sensing design flaw and PLC misconfiguration prevented the facility’s generator plant from receiving an automatic start signal to assume the critical load.”

Google’s UPSes therefore ran out of juice, but its generators didn’t start. The rest is history.

The search giant has figured out that its PLCs weren’t set up to handle the conditions it faced on this fateful day.

“PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant,” the status update reveals.

Once Google was able to reconnect to its power utility, it reprogrammed the PLC so it wouldn’t make the same mistake again.

The Big G has since made many changes to the electrical setup at europe-west-2-b and says it’s tested them and that they all work.

It’s also given itself two action items, one of which it describes as a “Communications Enhancement” that will see it “bolster notification speed by developing an automated alert-to-communication mechanism for location-impacting incidents.”

The other is to “expand platform-wide testing outcomes for infrastructure-level events.”

Once Google gets that done, perhaps it will be able to handle outages better – and if not, at least advise customers about its troubles more quickly. ®

#9981. Royal London plans IT outsourcing shake-up as staff brace for redundancies

IBM deal could see tech jobs shipped to India, with cuts expected before Christmas

Royal London plans to cut hundreds of IT jobs and shift work to India under an outsourcing deal with IBM, according to sources, with redundancies expected by the end of December.

Sources said Royal London's chief technology officer, James Sandell, told IT staff in September that the insurance and pensions giant was partnering with IBM to outsource a substantial portion of its technology operations. A consultation process was expected to follow.

A Royal London spokesperson told The Register: "Royal London has appointed IBM as its strategic technology infrastructure partner as it continues to develop its technology strategy. The partnership will give Royal London access to IBM’s specialist capability, scale and experience. Royal London will remain accountable for service delivery and regulatory requirements and continues to focus on ensuring continuity and quality of service for customers."

We asked Royal London how many UK IT roles it would retain and whether IBM would move work to India.

The exact number of jobs at risk remains unclear, although one Glassdoor review posted on October 6 claims that hundreds of positions in the company's technology operations division are being eliminated.

"A vast amount of knowledge is being lost by the business, a lot that is not yet documented due to constant years of recruitment freeze and workload volume," they wrote.

The reviewer also questioned whether management had grasped just how much work would be involved in handing operations over to IBM, particularly with already stretched teams being cut to a fraction of their former size.

Royal London replied to the Glassdoor review, acknowledging staff concerns about the changes, though it didn't comment on the claims about outsourcing and redundancies.

"We recognise that as Royal London is going through a period of transformation, this has raised questions and concerns for some colleagues," the company wrote. "We have established channels for colleagues to raise these, including through People Leaders and Colleague Representatives, and I encourage colleagues to use these routes to discuss their concerns."

Other October reviews questioned the handling of the outsourcing and Royal London's commitment to its mutual values.

An October 12 reviewer identifying themselves as an IT infrastructure employee said the company had historically offered good career prospects, before criticizing its new direction.

"Sudden outsourcing goes against all Royal London values," the reviewer wrote, adding that employees were questioning the company's direction amid reports of a hiring freeze and further potential cuts.

Another review, posted on October 20, suggested the IBM deal was the latest in a series of outsourcing decisions following an earlier move to transfer servicing jobs to South Africa.

"A mutual company but not mutual values when it comes to things like this," the reviewer claimed.

The planned cuts follow rising profits. Royal London reported adjusted group operating profit of £187 million in the first half of 2026, up 13 percent year-on-year.

Royal London has been keen to trumpet the benefits of its mutual structure, under which it is owned by customers rather than shareholders. Reporting the results in August, chief executive Barry O'Dwyer highlighted the £199 million distributed to eligible customers through ProfitShare in April.

"As a customer-owned business, when we do well, our customers share in that success," O'Dwyer said.

For employees facing redundancy before Christmas, the benefits of that success may be somewhat harder to appreciate.

#9978. SAP promises to open out data flows in both directions

New commitment to Apache Iceberg and expanded Databricks partnership point to battle ahead over context layer

SAP has taken meaningful steps in opening its data to bidrectional sharing across the enterprise, and in decoupling the advanced analytics needed for AI from its ERP upgrade path.

During a technical conference last week, the German software giant adopted native support for Apache Iceberg, the open table format, and extended its partnership with Databricks to bring data from legacy ERP systems into its modern cloud analytics platform.

"By putting [a] stake in the ground with Iceberg, we now have SAP moving from a very closed application storage model to an open lakehouse model," said Aaron Rosenbaum, Gartner senior director analyst, referring to the concept which brings together data lakes and warehouses.

Also important was the bridge between modern analytics in the cloud and on-prem or hosted legacy systems such as ECC, the ERP system broadly adopted by global companies. "SAP made a pretty big move in saying we're going to open this up, not just to S/4HANA Cloud [the latest ERP system], but ECC users. That coupling — leveraging of AI, leveraging a lakehouse for AI to the ERP upgrade lifecycle — was a problem," said Rosenbaum.

In May this year, SAP bought Dremio, a lakehouse platform built around Apache Iceberg, ending its previous preference for Databricks' Delta Sharing to bring together SAP data products with existing lakehouses bi-directionally.

At SAP's TedEd conference last week, SAP said its Business Data Cloud (BDC) – the "trusted data foundation for SAP Business AI Platform" – would now support native Apache Iceberg and a universal catalog powered by Apache Polaris, "providing an open and governed data foundation for users and [AI agent platform] Joule to consume data."

Together with SAP BDC Connect, the new tech policy will support platform interoperability with "zero-copy data sharing" across platforms from Databricks, Snowflake, Google, AWS, and Microsoft. The system would also continue to support Delta Lake, the alternative open table format from Databricks, SAP said.

With the integration of Dremio's SQL query engine, BDC users will also get access to relational databases including SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, and PostgreSQL without moving data, the vendor said.

During the same conference, Databricks – the lakehouse company born out of an Apache Spark platform – extended its partnership with SAP based on the previously announced SAP Databricks, which embeds the Databricks Data + AI Platform in BDC.

That "expanded scope" promises to make data from SAP applications available for consumption in the SAP Business Data Cloud engine of choice, including SAP Databricks. The vendor said that a manufacturer running finance and supply chain on SAP ECC on-premises, for example, could use SAP Application Data Foundation to bring historic order data into SAP Databricks, combining it with third-party data, and allowing data engineers to build demand-forecasting models on SAP's business semantics, without custom extraction pipelines. They can keep that work as they move to the cloud, Databricks suggested.

This being 2026, the hoped-for output from all of this data engineering is not just business insight, but automated action, by way of AI agents. SAP has its Joule AI assistant and agentic platform, while Databricks has Genie, and the two companies have promised to bring them together.

The increasing openness is good for users who will get more options in plotting a strategy to bring together enterprise data, leaving them pondering over where to put the business context layer, which vendors will no doubt fight to control, Rosenbaum said.

"You have the comment that they're going to bring Joule and Genie together in the future. This is pointing to a struggle that's going on throughout enterprises and throughout all the vendors about the context layer. I don't necessarily see that there's one winner. You do have different points of context within the transaction system and across the whole business, and they have been points of tension.

"Lack of single vendor lock-in is important. It's something that all the customers are struggling with: how do we build these context layers and deliver sort of consistent answers?"

SAP's shift in the direction of openness is likely to help users in this struggle, whether they choose to build the context layer within the ERP vendor's data platform using its semantic layer, or outside of it using tools from other vendors – there are plenty of companies offering help for those opening their wallets.

Nonetheless, whichever path users choose, a lot of work lies ahead. ®

#9975. Norway's aid agency pwned and all users' data is stolen

Norad said it cannot be sure that the details of those in 'conflict areas and authoritarian states' are safe or not

Norway's national aid agency, Norad, has confirmed that cyber criminals broke into its systems, stealing information about each and every registered user of its grant portal.

Norad, which coordinates Norway's assistance for foreign development, said that 20,614 registered individuals had their names and email addresses swiped, and information from at least three organizations' applications was "misdirected."

The agency clarified that the grant portal, which was launched in 2017, has 20,614 registered users, meaning all were affected, across 12,511 organizations.

In addition, the grant applications for at least three organizations are confirmed to be involved, though Norad said it may discover more as its investigation continues.

Torger Kjeldstad, director of digitalization at Norad, said "the attack is complex," and confirmed the agency has initiated a crisis team to manage it.

"We know a lot about what has happened, but to ensure that we have a complete overview of the attack, we are working to engage external experts in cybersecurity," he said.

"They will give us a detailed description of what information those who attacked the solution have gained access to."

Kjeldstad added that "it should be safe" to continue using Norad's services while it continues to probe what happened, and who was behind it.

Norad did not reveal many details about how the attack unfolded, other than saying that 27 accounts were compromised and were then used to gain access to the portal and the data in question.

The agency said the intrusion was detected on October 30, but did not offer any indication as to how long the attackers retained access to the grant portal.

It also refused to rule out that names of applicants in "conflict areas and authoritarian states" may have been included in the stolen data – it is not known if recipients would have also been registered users – and said it is approaching the matter "very seriously."

The grant portal, managed by Norad, which itself is part of Norway's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is responsible for handling applications from organizations across the world.

Recent case studies include support for independent, investigative journalism in Moldova, a country which routinely battles Russian propaganda and election interference, and backing for Ukrainian children and prisoners of war.

The issues Norad and the Norwegian government support, however, are wide-ranging – from access to healthcare for transgender people worldwide and Kenyan incubators for innovative transport solutions, to delivering aid to war-torn Gaza. ®

#9973. Beyond LoRA: Can you beat the most popular fine-tuning technique?

If you want to fine-tune an open model on your own data, you are probably interested in so-called parameter-efficient fine-tuning, in short PEFT. This term describes techniques that significantly reduce the memory requirement to fine-tune a model. Although there are dozens of these techniques, almost everyone chooses one called “LoRA”. In this blog post, we explore whether LoRA is really the best choice, what tools are available to make an informed decision, and how you can benefit from extending your horizon beyond LoRA.

There are countless open models available, but they often aren't quite good enough for your use case. Prompting may help, but it usually isn't enough. Rather than training a new model from scratch, you should consider fine-tuning an existing one.

Fine-tuning, however, is memory-hungry: you generally need enough memory to fit the whole model several times over. Quantization reduces a model's memory footprint, but quantized models can't be fine-tuned directly. So a set of techniques emerged to cut the memory needed for fine-tuning, called "parameter-efficient fine-tuning", or PEFT.

With PEFT, you can fine-tune a model using only a fraction of that memory and even fine-tune quantized models. It offers other advantages, such as tiny checkpoint sizes, greater resistance to catastrophic forgetting, and the ability to serve multiple fine-tunes from the same base model.

At Hugging Face, we develop the PEFT library, which implements many PEFT techniques behind a unified API and integrates well with the ecosystem, for example Transformers and Diffusers. It also supports multiple quantization methods, enabling further accessibility in parameter-efficient fine-tuning. PEFT provides a good starting point, whether you want to fine-tune on your own data or you're researching a new PEFT method.

One parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that emerged early and proved to be quite effective is called “Low Rank Adaptation”, or short “LoRA”. It works by adding a handful of parameters on top of the base model, freezing the base model weights, and only training those few parameters.

Among all PEFT techniques, LoRA is by far the most popular. Here are a few estimates:

Although these estimates are not perfect, the conclusion is nonetheless that LoRA is almost certainly by far the most common PEFT technique.

This could just mean that LoRA works best for everyone, and this fact is reflected in its usage statistics. There is, however, another possibility: LoRA was one of the earlier, popular PEFT techniques. So maybe its usage became self-reinforcing: LoRA has the highest visibility, the highest number of tutorials/examples, and it has the best support in downstream packages. Thus LoRA's popularity feeds on itself.

This all leads to the question: Are we all leaving performance on the table by shunning better techniques? After all, there are countless researchers whose papers claim their technique beats LoRA. Isn't that sufficient proof that we should go beyond LoRA in favor of newer techniques?

There are dozens of papers that investigate fine-tuning techniques other than LoRA. Just in the PEFT library, there are more than 40 distinct PEFT techniques at the time of writing (and numerous more when counting variations of PEFT techniques). For almost all of them, you will find researchers claiming that their technique beats LoRA according to their benchmarks.

The trouble with these claims is that researchers are under pressure to provide results that beat the existing benchmark. Even without ill intent, this can bias the results, e.g. by spending less time tuning the alternative techniques compared to the one proposed by the researchers. One study found, for instance, that LoRA can match supposedly better PEFT techniques by tuning the learning rate.

Another complication is that each paper chooses a different set of PEFT techniques to compare to, and a different set of benchmarks to run. And even if the same technique is compared on the same benchmark, the code is often not available or not easy to run yourself, which makes results hard to reproduce.

Overall, it's difficult to figure out the PEFT technique that works best for you by only checking paper results. Therefore, you might be tempted to just go with the default, LoRA.

At Hugging Face, we thought about how we can help users make informed decisions about which PEFT technique to use. With the PEFT library, we already provide a package that implements many PEFT techniques and exposes them with the same API. The next step is to provide benchmarks that can shed more light on the discussed issue.

We already had a benchmark that checks fine-tuning of LLMs on a math dataset for some time. This benchmark takes an LLM and fine-tunes it on chain-of-thought reasoning to produce the result to a mathematical question using a base model that is not instruction fine-tuned. The benchmark thus checks if the model can learn to perform mathematical reasoning and also to adjust the generated output to the expected format.

To extend our findings on another modality, we also added an image generation benchmark. This one tests whether the model can be fine-tuned to learn a new concept, a cat plushy, and generate it in new contexts without forgetting existing concepts.

All PEFT techniques are evaluated according to the exact same conditions: same base model, same dataset, same training and evaluation code, same hardware. As different users have different needs, we track more than just test performance. Besides VRAM usage, we track metrics like forgetting/drift, runtime, and checkpoint size. The results are designed to run on consumer hardware, and adding a new experiment only requires adding a new PEFT config and running a script.

Since we compare all PEFT techniques on equal footing and have no horse in the race, we believe that these benchmarks can draw an objective picture of how well different PEFT techniques work. We argue that if you have your own dataset, you can take a similar approach and take advantage of the PEFT library to evaluate multiple PEFT techniques.

After finishing the benchmark runs, we found that although LoRA works well, other PEFT methods can beat it on one or multiple axes and should thus be considered. Check the image below that compares the performance of LoRA and five other PEFT techniques.

One way to interpret the results above is to think in terms of tradeoffs, for example: How well does the model perform on the test set vs how much memory is needed to train it? If a PEFT technique cannot be beaten on both of these metrics at the same time by any other technique, it is on the Pareto Frontier. In other words: If you want better test accuracy, you need more memory, and if you want more memory efficiency, you have to give up on accuracy.

Let's take a closer look at the results for the LLM Math dataset benchmark. When it comes to test accuracy vs memory, we find that LoRA is indeed on the Pareto frontier. It achieves 53.2% test accuracy and requires 22.6 GB of VRAM at the peak. There are, however, other PEFT techniques on the Pareto Frontier. For instance, BEFT achieves 32.9% test accuracy and requires only 20.2 GB of memory at max. On the other end, we have Lily, which achieves 54.9% test accuracy but requires 25.6 GB of memory. Depending on what's more important to you, you may conclude that LoRA does not present the best tradeoff for you.

It is also worth noting that even though LoRA does well on this task, we're not talking about vanilla LoRA. On one side, we have LoRA with rank stabilized initialization, which is a technique to scale the LoRA contribution differently from the default initialization and provides very good test accuracy (53.2%). On the other end, we have LoRA-FA, which uses an optimizer specialized for LoRA that freezes part of the LoRA weights and is thus more memory efficient (20.2 GB). Normal LoRA only achieves an accuracy of 48.1% at 22.5 GB memory and should thus be avoided in favor of the alternatives.

Next let's take a look at the image generation benchmark. In the Hugging Face Space, choose “image-gen” in the “Select Task” dropdown to show the results. The goal of the task is to learn a new concept, namely a cat plushy, and generalize it to new prompts.

For this task, the main metric is “dino similarity”, which measures how much a generated image resembles the picture from a holdout test dataset, with higher values being better. As always, we also want to keep an eye on memory usage. When plotting the Pareto Frontier of these two metrics, we find that LoRA is below that frontier. Let's get concrete numbers: LoRA achieves a similarity score of 0.697 whereas OFT achieves 0.708; in terms of memory, LoRA requires 9.97 GB, and OFT requires 9.01 GB. Therefore, OFT strictly dominates LoRA on these metrics.

Of course, you should also check the other PEFT methods that are close to the Pareto frontier, as metrics can be subject to small variations due to randomness. Also, you should explore other metrics: is runtime performance important to you or do you care about the size of the checkpoints? Choose the relevant metric from the dropdown and the picture can change considerably. For the image generation benchmark, do inspect the generated sample images to get a vibe of the fine-tuned model's capability.

Objection: But the benchmarks favor one method over another!

One criticism that could be leveled at the PEFT benchmarks is that the choice of hyper-parameters may favor one technique over another. This is true, doing an exhaustive and fair hyper-parameter sweep with this many techniques is difficult. It is, however, very easy for everyone to contribute their own experiments to PEFT: If you believe that a specific PEFT technique can be improved by choosing different hyper-parameters, create a PR! We added instructions on how to do that. In a similar vein, if you want to contribute a completely new benchmark, reach out to us to discuss your idea.

Another problem with the benchmarks is that they may not fully reflect the capabilities of a specific PEFT technique. We make it possible to compare the techniques along many different dimensions and discover the best ones according to these tradeoffs. But it's impossible to capture all facets this way. For instance, one PEFT technique called Cartridges was developed to compress long prompts, which is not measured in the benchmarks. Other factors can also influence the choice, for instance:

The benchmarks cannot fully lift the responsibility to do your research, but they can be reasonable pointers.

Objection: But llama.cpp/vLLM/... only supports LoRA

A limitation of using a PEFT technique other than LoRA is that they don't get the broad support in downstream packages that LoRA sees. For example, if you want to serve the model using vLLM, only LoRA checkpoints can be loaded. Thankfully, PEFT now supports converting other adapters into LoRA. That way, you can convert a non-LoRA checkpoint into LoRA and use it in vLLM or other downstream packages.

To test this, we converted an image adapter using the GraLoRA technique into a LoRA checkpoint. The test scores were virtually identical after conversion (similarity 0.702 → 0.694, 0.260 → 0.269). Below are test images for the prompt “sks cat at the beach”:

At the moment, we haven't implemented conversion for all PEFT techniques, but if there is demand, we will expand the support.

While working on the PEFT package, we noticed that LoRA has a lot of momentum behind it, even though other PEFT techniques are potentially better. Therefore, we set out to add benchmarks to PEFT that could paint a more objective picture of how well different PEFT techniques perform on different metrics.

Given the results we found, we can confidently conclude that LoRA is not a bad choice at all, but there are potentially better choices. Especially when checking the image generation benchmark, LoRA is beaten by other techniques. We discussed that besides metrics, other considerations must be taken into account when choosing the right PEFT technique. However, even then, we are pushing PEFT further to achieve feature parity between LoRA and those other techniques.

Our journey is far from finished; we want to extend and improve the existing benchmarks, and we also plan to add more benchmarks in the future. We ensured that it is easy for the community to contribute, so if this is something you would like to do, please open an issue on the PEFT repository and let us know how you would like to contribute.

If you take away only one thing from this article, it is that LoRA should not be the automatic default when choosing a PEFT technique for your use case. Given the unified API provided by PEFT, changing from one PEFT technique to another is as easy as switching one config in your code. And even if you stick with LoRA, check out all the variants that are supported in PEFT: DoRA, rs-LoRA, LoRA-FA etc. Give these other techniques a try and you might be pleasantly surprised.

Example: Changing from LoRA to OFT using PEFT:

Compare PEFT methods and view Pareto trade‑offs

What about DEFT?It adapts a pre-trained weight matrix by decomposing its update into two components with two trainable matrices: (1) a projection onto the complement of a low-rank subspace spanned by a low-rank matrix, and (2) a low-rank update. The single trainable low-rank matrix defines the subspace, while the other trainable low-rank matrix enables flexible parameter adaptation within that subspace.

GitHub https://github.com/MAXNORM8650/DEFT

would you like to make a PEFT PR for this?

OFT had a version 2, skipped over version1. Which one did you guys test?

It's the updated version 2 of OFT: https://github.com/huggingface/peft/pull/2575.

Was there a reason EMLoC and the Drag-and-Drop LLMs methods weren't included in the comparison?

We only included techniques that are implemented in PEFT, and those two are not implemented.
