#9952. GNU Mes and the 0.28 release

From the series: GNU Mes interpreter speedup

It’s been a while since the latest blog post in the series but we have been working very hard behind the scenes 1. This means I’ll probably forget a few things from all we did, but there’s a good reason for that: we were making a release.

This is the first official and serious release I make as a (co-)maintainer, and the whole thing makes me uncomfortable. Even though people treat me as an expert programmer sometimes, there are many things in programming that I struggle a lot with. The first one, that I think I improved on in the last few years, is writing software from scratch. The second is delivering things to people.

This is normal, as all my career has been focused on R&D and that’s the way I’ve been trained to work. In the case of this specific release, something inside me still thinks my most valuable contribution was that: the idea and demonstration that this attempt could work.

Most of my career has been based on learning in a short time period the right amount of information so I can achieve a reasonable result. Then I normally move on to the next project.

Thinking about that, trying to read through my feelings, I started to realize more and more that whatever that drives me is pushing me to somewhere else, maybe to those parts I struggle more with…

Releasing code is important. It’s the only way to make people actually enjoy the result of your work. I have no problem to admit I struggle with this.

As an R&D guy I’ve always considered myself an “enabler”. I do something, I show how it is done and let people learn from it and actually implement it. That’s fine in some contexts but it has been driving me to some level of frustration recently, as the size of the projects I take part in grow.

An example of this is the RISC-V bootstrap on Guix. I spent a couple of years of my life working on it. We made a working bootstrap for live-bootstrap. But it’s not yet included in Guix because I delegated the final step. Now, even after the years I spent on that, all the sleepless nights and everything, it’s something I cannot enjoy fully2, and you cannot enjoy at all.

This “my job here is done” mentality is not enough for me anymore.

The kind of projects I do now deserve something else. I deserve better.

In Mes I had like 300 commits in a branch, pretty ugly, doing, undoing and redoing some stuff over and over again. The whole codebase was upside down, the commit messages were sometimes good and sometimes lacking, I had fixup commits that fixed things that were changed so much the amount of conflicts the reordering produced was overwhelming… It was a mess. It was me trying new things, learning and cleaning things up as I went. My arborescent thought process at its fullest.

In my usual way of doing things, I decided to promise NlNet a release, something I’ve never done before 3.

Once the bytecode adventure was done, showing some good performance improvement was possible and that Janneke made me a co-maintainer, it was the only acceptable thing to do.4

But, if I wanted to do it, I would need to slow down.

In the last part of the bytecode adventures, you remember how we included Popsyntax, and we reworked the whole macro expansion game. That wasn’t me, but Tim Sample.

I don’t remember very well how he joined my efforts here but I guess I bothered him with questions because he’s a long term Mes contributor and he’s also the author of Popsyntax, the Germ scheme implementation and many interesting things more.

He decided to start over. Chose a Mes release and walked through my steps. Removed the macro expander from the internals and wrote one in Scheme. From there, the direction was set.

I worked through the huge branch that I had, removing the stuff that turned out to be unnecessary, and he took over the git history, and made sure that every single commit was working.

I cannot imagine how many conflicts the guy has been resolving. But damn this looks good now.

This week, I released GNU Mes 0.28. The first release that I do as a GNU maintainer.

Janneke has been guiding me through the whole process — including the part of publishing the website to GNU using CVS5. I’m sure I would’ve never been able to figure out everything on my own. What a ride it has been!

But after more than a year of work, I’m very happy that most of the comments on the release have been positive, specially the ones from people that I worked with and I have a huge respect for.6

But, what will you find in GNU Mes 0.28 that we didn’t mention in the blog yet?

First of all, the main difference from the earlier blogpost is now Mes can be compiled with both M2-Planet and MesCC, and also with GCC as before.

It’s a tricky process, because the error reporting is very limited (I’m being benevolent here), and I was being a very nasty boy with some gotos inside switch statements. After some wrestling with allowed C syntax, I figured it out.

M2-Planet is limited, and we had to leave some things out. When Mes is compiled with M2-Planet it doesn’t have support for errors (aka exceptions) and those abort the interpreter, this is because M2-Planet’s C library doesn’t include setjmp. The stack operations had also to be rewritten as functions for M2-Planet, as the macros with array access were too complex for it. With that, Mes is a little bit slower when compiled with M2-Planet.

None of those are a big deal because that’s only the starting point of the bootstrap process and Mes is rebuilt with MesCC right after it.

The 0.28 release has been tested on real RISC-V hardware that I have access to,7 uncovering a few issues here and there in the Mes C Library.

First, the assembly parts that take care of program initialization in RISC-V (written by myself a few years ago, when I was working on the bootstrap) were broken.

setjmp and longjmp that we use for error handling in Mes, and were not used before, are also faulty. Because of this, the RISC-V version of Mes in the bootstrap, when built with MesCC that is, does not support errors until the issue is fixed.

I also found some extra stuff because GCC 14 decided that implicit function declaration warnings should become errors, breaking the bootstrap that we didn’t test in a very long time in RISC-V, first, because hardware unavailability and, second, because Qemu is also faulty for RISC-V.

There is still a known issue with M2-Planet-built Mes that explodes when it calls strcpy, this can be triggered running (procedure-disassemble map) in the REPL. We didn’t manage to fix this yet.

Tim reworked the macro expansion and made a simple and understandable initial macro expander in Scheme.

With that ready, many things started to fall off naturally.

Most of our driving issues simply disappeared. The macro expander takes the steering wheel from the start, giving us zero garbage collection issues during boot.

The earlier macro expander I wrote in C had to also drive execution, which could possibly call the garbage collector, killing all the C pointers that we had. The new macro expander does everything from Scheme, so no pointers are lost: gc_preserve and gc_release are gone. The boot-done! mark is gone, too.

As Tim started from scratch, all the API is way cleaner, and our initial driver is as simple as:

We can now use the stack for preservation, as it doesn’t happen that often, and the initial driver is a minimal loop that iterates through the few top-level expressions the initial boot file has (the macro expander). The rest of the program is run from Scheme.

Continuing with macro expansion, even if in previous posts we talked about Popsyntax integration, we decided to leave that out the release for now. We focused on having a faster interpreter with a new VM.

Keeping macro expansion simple, we are faster than ever.

These are the updated numbers from the 0.28 release comparing with the previous 0.27.2 bugfix release, released a week before.

This is running in my Tuxedo laptop from 2020:

You can see the times are similar to the nosyntax (it’s basically the same) branch we described in the previous post.

Take in account the numbers are tricky because mescc-mes means Mes building itself running MesCC. From one version to the other Mes changed, making it a little bit larger (+200 LoC), which means it should take longer to compile. The new version overcomes that, and even achieves a 40% reduction on execution time.

The fib benchmark is the most savage to me. There you can easily see how running has become way cheaper. On the other hand, mescc-hello shows how building a small hello-world program is more expensive, as Mes now needs to compile the whole MesCC to bytecode. When running MesCC for longer, like in a real program (mescc-mes), shows the startup time is compensated by far by the execution speed.

In summary, we got exactly what we were aiming for: a change so big the benchmarks don’t need to be precise. An improvement you can just feel by running Mes.

When I wrote the bytecode compiler I added a very annoying warning that complained about possibly unbound variables when you did something like:

This was later removed because the amount of warnings it was producing was really overwhelming and they didn’t really give us any useful information.

But! When I tested the bootstrapping process during development I realized they appeared twice. This led me to find the build scripts were compiling each file twice by accident.

So now, we are not just x2 faster in Mes. The bootstrapping is also x2 faster thanks to the annoying warnings!

Comparing to the code in the earlier post in the series, the released code has proper support for values and call-with-values that I thought I did right but I didn’t, really.

According to R7RS standard, the values procedure returns its arguments as values to the current continuation. If the continuation only accepts one value, only the first value is sent to the continuation. That’s what a regular continuation would do. With call-with-values the producer is called in a continuation that accepts multiple values that go directly to the consumer procedure.

If you take a look to the Guile case, that’s exactly how it works. Chibi takes the pragmatic approach not implementing the value discard and uses values just as a container. That’s what I implemented in the previous blogpost, but in the release I managed to do the standards compliant case, and make a REPL that now supports multiple return values, like Guile does:

The tricky part of values is solved with a very primitive support for continuation marks.

When call-with-values is called, the current frame is labeled with a mark, saying it accepts multiple values. When values is called, it checks the current mark in order to decide if it should keep or discard its arguments. It looks like this:

This whole thing works very well thanks to proper tail-calls, which reuse the frames so the marks are right in the current frame all the time. It’s clean and simple.

It also uses the simplest approach possible. The %values builtin wraps values in a list, adding an special car to it. core:cdr can be used to extract the list of values back from the wrapper.

Of course, we could do this “better” just putting the values raw in the stack, but this is good enough for now. If Chibi can get away with doing less, we should be fine with this.

I would never solve this issue if it wasn’t because some random research I did, encouraged by Tim and all the knowledge he has about Scheme implementations.

I was looking at a few papers on delimited continuations, like “Final Shift for Call/cc: Direct Implementation of Shift and Reset” by Martin Gasbichler and Michael Sperber, when Tim told me about his approach in Germ using continuation marks.

With that in mind, I made a very fast sketch on how would continuation marks look like and I realized that was more than enough for the values implementation I was struggling with when I saw the Mes tests (which I didn’t bother to run during the research time) started to fail for the value discard case.

I ended up using only the most minimal thing for it, but I hope to take it a little bit further in the future and make a proper continuation marks based Delimited Continuation support for Mes.

There are many things happening in this release. The diff is huge. But mostly you have been following the effort during the latest blogposts so there’s no need to go deeply in detail.

You saw me re-write the garbage collector, the macro expander, the driver, the builtin implementation, vectors and structs, values, continuations … Some of the code is gone (gc, macro expander and driver, the first implementation of continuations) but the knowledge stays. I basically visited every single corner in this interpreter.

I’m used to hop from one thing to the next. That’s the R&D me again. Now that I know this software the best, I don’t want to just go do anything else. Now I’m the best position to improve it further.

My goal for the future is to improve Mes in all those areas that I found it could be improved but I couldn’t focus on.

Delimited continuations are the best way to represent continuations in an stack based VM like the one I added to Mes. They are more lightweight, better for the GC, and they are composable, allowing for more sophisticated control. Guile supports them, so it would also help us get a step closer to Guile.

Pointer tagging could be a huge deal for speed and reduced memory usage in contrast to the tagged union approach Mes has. To give you an example, in a 64 bit machine each value is at least 24 bytes, including characters. This means if you (string->list "Hello") the result takes 24 bytes per cons cell, i.e per element, plus 24 bytes per character. Pointer tagging would put the bytes for the characters inside the pointers the cons cells have, reducing the total memory to just what the list needs (half of the previous case) and removing the need to access memory again to get the value of the characters.

With some type punning we could also revisit a few data structures we had some trouble with (mostly frames and templates) and make them flat and easy for the CPU to cache and access with no indirection.

In the case of the Scheme to bytecode compiler, just making it slightly better than the dumbest thing possible can make Scheme code fly: builtin inlining, avoiding boxing of non-mutated values… There are many things we can do while keeping complexity under control.

Some GC improvement is also needed, maybe with a simple generational-style garbage collector (does that exist?), at least for a few things like symbols and globals that are never collected it could improve the performance. Even if it doesn’t, we could always use some cleanup in the GC, which is very error prone now.

Those are low-hanging fruits that the new architecture made more accessible. If I just stop here they could be lost.

On the mid term, with all this together and all the improvements Janneke is doing, we could bring MesCC to the next level as a C99 compiler written in Guile that can be incidentally run in Mes.

On the long term, the GNU Mes project would become a very powerful bootstrapping toolchain for languages of any kind.

The GNU Mes development repository is now hosted in Codeberg, under the Mes organization8:

And we have opened an IRC channel at libera.chat: #mes

I tend to listen to my heart, my curiosity, gut feeling, or whatever you want to call it. That has pushed me to do uncomfortable things.

It is daunting, but it has been really rewarding.

The same way Free Software has made me learn how to program, GNU Mes has been an amazing training camp for the skills I was lacking: reading CS papers, preparing a release, writing code from scratch…

The project made me understand slowing down is sometimes the best way to go forward, and that I have to be more comfortable switching gears.

This is not just programming advice, but a general approach to life that I’m starting to understand as I get older —and hopefully wiser.9

Thankfully I’m surrounded by people I can learn from, and they bring the best version of me. All the crazy things that I attempt would have been impossible without the people I find in the process.

In this specific case of Mes, I’m very happy with the team we have. They supported me throughout the whole process, but specially during the release, when I was more insecure. I’m sure the next time I’ll be more comfortable slowing down and doing things right.

Thanks to them for the help, inspiration and support.

Thanks to NlNet and NGI for the trust and the chance to work in important but not-very-popular projects. Without funding, none of this is possible.

I hope we can continue to work all together for some time more.

We closed this one well. There’s no reason to stop here, though.

The “GNU Mes speedup effort” project has been funded through NGI Zero Core, a fund established by NLnet with financial support from the European Commission’s Next Generation Internet program.

I have mixed feelings with it, really. From time to time I come back to it and I cannot figure out how to do it. Then something else comes and I have to leave it. It’s a shame. ↩

Of something I’ve never did before (an optimization work) in something that I never worked before (a scheme interpreter). ↩

The other possibility was to chicken out, give Janneke the branch and disappear. ↩

Also, getting an email by RMS himself congratulating me for the release has made me a little bit emotional. Not gonna lie. I’m sure he does that for every release, but I’m a weak man. ↩

Thanks to my friend Iban for the SSH access. Siuuuh! ↩

My repository has been transferred to Mes. ↩

#9951. Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

As artificial intelligence squeezes early-career learning opportunities, capture-the-flag contests could be one way to help pick up the slack.

Artificial intelligence (AI) may be gobbling up entry-level jobs and learning opportunities for security practitioners, but it can't erase the value of hands-on experience with enterprise systems and security tools.

No matter how much agentic action cybersecurity teams embed into their security operations center (SOC) and the rest of their programs, smart people have to backstop that work. And the only way these "humans-in-the-loop" can do that capably is if they build up the kind of judgment that's best learned from the school of hard knocks.

The problem? With SOC tier 1 analysts becoming an endangered species and bug bounty programs on the ropes from a glut of AI submissions, the chances are dwindling for security newbies to rack up real-world experience.

There's no great fix to this career pipeline problem just yet, but some of the answers might be found in one of the industry's age-old mechanisms for both camaraderie and skill-building: the trusty capture-the-flag (CTF) competition.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

"CTFs give passionate talent the opportunity to grow and learn in ways that they might not have at their day jobs," says Jason Walker, a security engineer by day at software-as-a-service firm Five9. An avid CTF competitor, he won the Sentinels League competition sponsored and run by SentinelOne, beating two other finalists from a field of thousands of competitors worldwide. Besides street cred, Walker picked up a $5,000 prize for his efforts and a $10,000 donation in his name to his charity of choice, Trans Lifeline.

The livestreamed event offered up the spectacle and fun of an e-sports competition, but it may hold deeper clues as to how the industry can keep refreshing its talent pool in the coming years. As Walker puts it, CTFs are the ultimate way to expose both new and experienced cyber professionals to a wider range of problems and technologies.

"CTFs have helped me be a lot more versatile," he says. "If your company is running well and your program is mature, you aren't going to necessarily be firefighting new things every week. You're not going to be exposed to every new technique and threat. Doing CTF events and other hands-on training is a really important way to make sure you can stay up to date."

CTF competitions come in many shapes and sizes, but they fundamentally challenge players to find hidden pieces of data called "flags" buried inside intentionally vulnerable systems. Most fall into one of two formats: Jeopardy-style events, the kind Sentinels League runs, hand out standalone puzzles across categories such as Web exploitation, forensics, and cryptography, with points awarded per solve. Attack-defense events ask each team to defend its own vulnerable network while trying to break into everyone else's.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

The attack-defense format took shape at DEF CON's CTF, which started in 1996 and is still the event most associated with it. It has sprung forth a wellspring of CTF formats that range from grassroots industry events to big vendor-sponsored competitions like Sentinels League.

Sentinels League grew out of ThreatOps, a set of internal games SentinelOne's solutions engineers have run since 2020 to teach customers how to hunt through telemetry for hidden flags. This year's championship built on that with four games — Endpoint, Cloud, SIEM, and AI — spread across 12 weeks of qualifiers between June and October

The opening player pool of 2,236 entrants came from more than 100 countries, competing for a total prize pool of $100,000. Smaller prizes were dispensed across the qualifier and regional events, with the bigger prizes kept on reserve for the final, which was held in conjunction with SentinelOne's annual OneCon event.

Ryan O'Grady, director of SE operations at SentinelOne, says the firm invests the money in the prizes and the considerable logistics of running such a big event as a way to give back to the community, to build up expertise and exposure to its platform, and as a recruiting tool.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

Whether motivated for the prizes or the training, the appetite for the event keeps growing. This year's drew enough interest that the company had to get a bigger ballroom to accommodate spectators.

Sentinels League is just one example of what a CTF looks like amid a much broader spectrum of competitions available. On CTFtime, the volunteer-run archive that tracks the hobbyist side of the scene, last year's calendar alone listed more than 200 individually organized events, with active teams from countries spanning every populated continent.

DEF CON CTF, often called the World Series of hacking, pulled 673 teams through its 2026 qualifiers before finals in Las Vegas this August. The National Cyber League, a nonprofit circuit O'Grady competes in, drew more than 7,500 students from 670 schools and universities this past spring. Kaspersky continues to run its own wildly popular SAS CTF out of Bali.

Other more academic events, such as New York University's CSAW and Carnegie Mellon's picoCTF, run versions aimed at students. Larger consulting firms, such as KPMG, use the format to scout corporate recruits.

In spite of the obvious demand for CTFs evident in the number of events held worldwide and the thousands of participants willing to sink their personal time into these pursuits, many security pundits worry about what AI is going to do to the purpose and purity of these competitions.

CTF organizers are thinking deeply about what this means for their rule books and how they enforce them. RITSEC's 2026 rules ban using AI to autonomously solve challenges outright, calling it against the spirit of the competition. Meantime, CSAW leaned into AI, this year creating an entire track built around using large language models (LLMs) to solve past CTF problems.

DEF CON CTF's 2026 qualifier split the difference. It barred fully autonomous AI teams but let human competitors use AI tools as long as a person stayed meaningfully in charge, requiring every team to label itself No AI, Low AI, or Human-Led AI on the public scoreboard.

A recent study of hundreds of Hack The Box machines released between 2017 and 2025 found solve times dropped roughly 16% a year, with the steepest declines after 2022. The hardest tier of challenges went from a 15-hour median solve down to about five, according to penetration tester Jacob Krell of Suzu Labs, who did the analysis.

He's not the only one worried. An academic study earlier this year from IBM Research and the College of William & Mary pitted 41 participants in a live, on-site CTF against four autonomous AI agents. It found that those agents placed second overall, ahead of most of the human teams competing.

Findings like these are enough to get firms like OtterSec, a blockchain security firm, to make noise about how to "save" CTFs. This summer the firm launched a $100,000 "Save CTFs Fund" to bankroll new formats that stay meaningful as AI keeps improving.

SentinelOne's O'Grady doesn't buy the death-of-CTFs talk. In his view, AI just forces organizers to redesign CTFs so they still force a human to think laterally, AI assistance or not.

AI may not be killing creative CTFs anytime soon, but it is definitely making cybersecurity's career ladder wobble. In the process it may actually be making CTFs even more crucial.

SANS Institute polled nearly 1,000 security leaders and found unclear career progression to be one of the top hiring challenges, cited by 32%, more than triple the rate last year. Only one-quarter of organizations say they have a clearly defined career path, and entry-level jobs that used to train the next generation of defenders are diminishing. SOC and security analyst roles lead the AI-driven cuts, down 32%. Threat intelligence analysts are next, at 26%, with incident responders close behind, at 22%.

Bug bounty programs are buckling under AI's pressure. At the start of the year, maintainers of the open source project Curl shut down their program after a massive influx of junk AI submissions. HackerOne paused its Internet Bug Bounty program in April after a wave of low-quality, AI-assisted reports flooded in. And this month Google Bug Hunters also paused its open source bounty program due to similar problems.

These are all blows for cyber career progression, as bug bounty problems were another great place for security professionals to flex their skills publicly and for newcomers to gain a foothold into the industry.

As long as CTF organizers can keep their competitions relevant, these events will remain a valuable puzzle piece in the skills training picture for the industry, alongside other important hands-on challenges like cyber ranges.

"With LLMs basically sweeping the table on bug bounties, it's become even harder than it already was for people to get out there, show off their skills, and get their name out there," O'Grady says. "AI has only increased the importance of CTF events like this."

#9950. Tobacco company got smoked by leaving secret recipes on a file share

They denied the data was real...then removed it

Welcome once again to PWNED, where all of the security victims are self-owned. Today, we celebrate a company that makes a supremely unhealthy product having a supremely unhealthy security posture.

Our tale of terrible data management, once again, comes courtesy of professional pen tester and red teamer Dahvid Schloss. Assigned to find flaws in the network of a tobacco company, Schloss stumbled onto some very poorly protected trade secrets.

Schloss started by probing the network with tools like Metasploit, a popular open-source pen testing app. Surprisingly, the company’s Trend Micro antivirus did not issue an alert even as he was scanning the network for vulnerabilities. He compared the process to shooting a machine gun and having no one hear it.

"I'm running through this environment, and I'm basically just using the loudest toys and tools you can imagine," he told The Register. It seemed as if the client simply didn't care much. "I'm feeling like there's not a whole lot of value that I'm providing here."

Schloss then asked his boss what else he could do to make his findings more useful and compelling to the client.

"My senior manager turns to me and goes 'Think about what is important to this organization. If it got leaked, how detrimental would it be to their business?'" Schloss said. "I’m thinking it’s a products company. Maybe their recipes."

Schloss began searching for network file shares that allowed unauthenticated or anonymous access. After discovering an open share, he scanned it using the network mapping tool Nmap. The scan revealed that ports 139 and 445 were open, indicating that the system was running the Windows SMB file sharing protocol. Despite hosting sensitive IT and HR records, this specific file share had no access restrictions and was completely exposed to every employee in the company.

Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential." He found files in there which were named recipe, the product name, the sub product name, and the date. He opened one file and discovered that it had information about how that tobacco product was made, including the weight and volume and what percentage of each chemical it had inside.

The file was marked with red letters at the top that said "Confidential" and another set at the bottom that said "Do not share."

“I think we found a smoking gun here. This is pretty bad,” Schloss said. He noted that anyone on the network could simply use Windows Explorer to find the file.

Schloss downloaded the file, thinking he'd be able to show it to the company to prove that the data could be exfiltrated.

But his manager asked him to delete the downloaded file, because it was such sensitive information that he shouldn't retain a copy. This would later harm his ability to show that it had ever existed at all.

He then told the security team at the tobacco company what he had found, expecting them to lock down all the recipe files. But when he returned to the site the next morning, he got a big surprise: His contact came by and told him that the recipes he found were not real. He denied the files had ever existed and that there was a security problem at all.

"And we're just kind of baffled because we're like, what? What are you talking about? This is clearly a recipe you guys have," Schloss said. "It's in the right department. It's in the right folder structure, it's named the right way. Anybody who saw this would consider this a recipe."

He listed the recipe files in his security report, but the security people at the tobacco company vehemently denied that the files were real or that he had seen a real recipe. They continued arguing about it for a year and Schloss could not show them the recipe file he had downloaded because he had been forced to erase it.

"The funny thing is, I went back and checked towards the end of the engagement to see if those files are still in that folder. And no, they were gone, they were deleted or moved, or something," he said. "So there was obviously some truth behind it, but they wanted to deny the finding." ®

#9949. Accelerating Transformers Fine-Tuning with NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel

HuggingFace Transformers has become the foundation of the open-source AI ecosystem, and the recent Transformers v5 release strengthened it with first-class support for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, now the dominant architecture for frontier models. v5 ships the MoE foundations: expert backends, dynamic weight loading, and distributed execution that make MoE extensible and easy to build on.

NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel is an open library part of the NVIDIA NeMo framework for building custom generative AI models at scale. NeMo AutoModel builds cleanly on top of v5, adding Expert Parallelism, DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch, and TransformerEngine kernels, and it leans on v5's dynamic weight loading to bring those optimizations to a broad and growing set of model families. The payoff is 3.4-3.7x higher training throughput and 29-32% less GPU memory on fine-tuning MoE models than native Transformers v5, using the same from_pretrained() API: a single import line, with no other code changes.

This blog details how this combination works and how users can fine-tune MoE models faster without changing their APIs.

The rise of MoE models has introduced new challenges to efficient training: Routing tokens across hundreds of experts, fusing expert matmuls into a single kernel, sharding weights across GPUs, and overlapping communication with computation all require infrastructure beyond what a general-purpose library provides out of the box.

Transformers v5 (“v5”) introduced first-class MoE support such as expert backends, dynamic weight loading, and tensor parallel plans for distributed execution. In addition, v5 made distributed training first-class by integrating PyTorch's DeviceMesh directly into from_pretrained().

NeMo AutoModel builds on top of v5 by subclassing AutoModelForCausalLM, and adding Expert Parallelism (EP), DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch, and TransformerEngine kernels. DeepEP is the piece v5 doesn't have yet: it overlaps communication with expert compute. And because NeMo AutoModel rides v5's reversible weight conversion to load each model, it can focus its engineering on these reusable core ops instead of per-model checkpoint plumbing, while save_pretrained() still emits standard HF checkpoints that tools like vLLM and SGLang can load.

The next section walks through how the two work together and the performance gains we measured, from full fine-tuning NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B across 16 nodes down to single-node models such as Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B.

One of NeMo AutoModel's goals is API compatibility with HuggingFace Transformers to enable open-source community. NeMoAutoModelForCausalLM subclasses AutoModelForCausalLM, so any code that works with HF models works with AutoModel too.

Here's what loading a model looks like in both. Only the import changes:

That single import does a lot of work. For popular MoE architectures like Qwen3, NVIDIA Nemotron, GPT-OSS, and DeepSeek V3, NeMo AutoModel ships hand-tuned implementations with TransformerEngine attention, fused linear layers, and custom expert kernels. For everything else, it falls back to vanilla HF while still applying optimizations like Liger kernel patching, among others. And whichever path it takes, the resulting model is ready to scale: pass a device_mesh and you have multi-GPU training without further rewrites.

Where NeMo AutoModel really shines is scaling MoE models to multi-GPU training. To train Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B with Expert Parallelism across 8 GPUs, one adds the distributed mesh configuration:

This gives speed, scalability and memory-optimizations with FSDP2, Expert Parallelism, TransformerEngine kernels and DeepEP dispatch, all from a from_pretrained() call.

We evaluated NeMo AutoModel in two regimes: full fine-tuning a frontier-scale 550B model across 16 nodes, and training two 30B MoE models on a single node. The 550B result shows why Expert Parallelism is essential at scale; the 30B results quantify the per-GPU speedup over Transformers v5.

Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B is a 550B-parameter hybrid model shipping with Mamba2, LatentMoE, and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). We benchmark a full fine-tune: every parameter is updated and the Adam optimizer state is materialized, which at this scale spans 16 H100 nodes (128 GPUs).

Why there is no Transformers v5 column. Transformers v5 runs out of memory at this scale, so there is no v5 number to report here. AutoModel's Expert Parallelism shards the experts across GPUs to bring the footprint within budget, which is what lets the full fine-tune run. The 30B comparisons below show the same advantage where v5 fits.

We benchmarked three approaches on a single node with 8x H100 80GB GPUs: HF Transformers v4 (hub code), HF Transformers v5 (with best available optimizations), and NeMo AutoModel (EP=8 + custom kernels).

A note on the routing gate. The NeMo AutoModel numbers below use a balanced routing gate, which forces tokens to be distributed uniformly across experts. This emulates the ideal operating point an MoE is trained toward: a well-trained model's load-balancing loss drives expert utilization to near-uniform, so balanced routing reflects the steady-state a real workload converges to (and removes the straggler noise that random dummy tokens otherwise inject into expert parallelism). v4/v5 run their native router on the same dummy tokens. The balanced gate therefore measures NeMo AutoModel at its target MoE operating point, and the v4/v5 columns reflect their out-of-the-box behavior.

Why v4 deadlocks: Transformers v4 stores Qwen3 MoE experts as a ModuleList of 128 individual MLP modules, each separately FSDP-wrapped. The forward pass uses a data-dependent loop that only iterates experts that received tokens. With different data per rank, different ranks skip different experts, causing mismatched FSDP AllGather/ReduceScatter collectives and an indefinite hang. Transformers v5 fixes this by storing experts as fused 3D parameter tensors (no per-expert modules, no per-expert FSDP collectives).

v4 config: trust_remote_code=True (NVIDIA's hub modeling code). The hub code's expert loop is FSDP-safe (iterates all experts regardless of token assignment), so it doesn't deadlock like Qwen3 v4.

The 3.4-3.7x speedup from NeMo AutoModel over Transformers v5 comes from three sources:

Expert Parallelism reduces memory pressure. EP=8 distributes expert weights across GPUs, cutting the per-GPU MoE footprint by 8x. For Qwen3, this drops peak memory from 68.2 GiB to 48.1 GiB (-29%). For Nemotron Nano, it drops from 62.1 GiB to 42.5 GiB (-32%), freeing headroom for larger batch sizes or longer sequences.

DeepEP fuses communication with computation. Instead of separate AllGather/ReduceScatter collectives for expert routing, DeepEP fuses token dispatch and combines into optimized GPU kernels, overlapping communication with expert computation.

TransformerEngine kernels accelerate core operations. TE's fused attention, linear layers, and RMSNorm implementations provide consistent speedups over their PyTorch/Flash Attention equivalents across all layer types, not just MoE layers.

One of the most impactful features in Transformers v5 is the experts_implementation parameter, which includes three expert backends:

The grouped_mm backend is the key training optimization: instead of looping over experts one by one, it sorts tokens by their assigned expert and executes a single fused grouped matrix multiplication.

NeMo AutoModel takes this further. For models with custom implementations, it uses DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch combined with grouped GEMM kernels and TransformerEngine linear layers. The progression looks like:

In NeMo AutoModel, the expert backend is configured through BackendConfig:

Transformers v5 also ships an Expert Parallelism path. It shards expert weights across GPUs. The GroupedGemmParallel style loads only each device's local experts, and RouterParallel routes tokens and combines results with an all_reduce. It's neatly built on v5's existing tensor-parallel machinery. Enabling it makes the model's tp_plan return its expert plan, so expert parallelism shares the device budget with data parallelism (ep × dp = world_size). For the single-node 30B benchmarks here, we found plain data-parallel v5 (dp=8, ep=1) to be the fastest v5 configuration, so that's the v5 setup we report.

NeMo AutoModel takes a complementary approach tuned for multi-GPU MoE training. It makes EP its own parallelism dimension, a dedicated moe_mesh alongside (rather than carved from) the data-parallel mesh, using PyTorch's DTensor with Shard(0). Because the expert mesh is orthogonal to data parallelism, the two compose on the same devices. On 8 GPUs NeMo AutoModel runs ep=8 and dp=8 together, so every GPU trains on its own data shard while holding only 1/8 of the experts. Expert weights are physically sharded across GPUs along the expert dimension.

With ep_size=8 on 8 GPUs, each GPU holds only 1/8 of the expert parameters. For a model like Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B with ~55 GiB of expert weights, EP reduces the per-GPU expert footprint from ~55 GiB to ~6.8 GiB, making training possible where FSDP-only approaches run out of memory.

On top of EP, NeMo AutoModel integrates DeepEP that fuses the token routing into optimized GPU kernels, and delivers significant speedups when combined with grouped GEMM for grouped expert computation. In our large-scale MoE benchmarks, DeepEP + grouped GEMM reduced cost per iteration by 47% on the full DeepSeek V3 671B model compared to all-gather + looped expert baselines.

Transformers v5 also introduced a dynamic weight loading system through WeightConverter and WeightRenaming. This enables MoE checkpoint to be stored in fused 3D tensors for more efficient execution. The WeightConverter applies composable operations to transform checkpoint tensors on-the-fly during from_pretrained().

NeMo AutoModel is a direct consumer of this v5 API. Over 20 model types use this mechanism through MODELS_REQUIRING_TENSOR_MERGING, including Mixtral, Qwen2 MoE, Qwen3 MoE, DeepSeek V2/V3, OLMoE, and more. The conversions are fully reversible: save_pretrained() produces standard HF-format checkpoints that any downstream tool can load.

To try NeMo AutoModel, please visit our official documentation page to get started.

NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel is the natural next step for HuggingFace users scaling up model training. By building directly on Transformers v5, AutoModel provides a zero-friction upgrade path: change one import line and get a model instance that is more than three times as fast.

On Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, this delivers 3.4-3.7x higher training throughput with 29-32% less GPU memory compared to the best Transformers v5 configuration. And because true Expert Parallelism shards experts across GPUs, the same path scales up to full fine-tuning a 550B model like Nemotron 3 Ultra across 16 nodes, the regime where Expert Parallelism becomes essential to fit the model in memory. Because NeMo AutoModel checkpoints are standard HF-format safetensors, you can deploy them on inference frameworks like vLLM and SGLang.

The code, configs, and benchmark scripts are all available in the NeMo AutoModel repository.

Core contributors to this work, listed alphabetically by last name: Adil Asif, Hemil Desai, Alexandros Koumparoulis, and Huiying Li.

#9948. Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series discusses some of the trends and topics from Cybersecurity Awareness Month, from using AI for better training to educating next-generation workforces on modern risks and emerging threats.

AI is changing the concept of cybersecurity awareness in more ways than one.

In the latest installment of our monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea, and Dark Reading's Rob Wright discuss some of the trends they've observed during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, which has shifted during the AI era with the emergence of news threats as well as revamped defense strategies.

As we’ve seen in years past, cybersecurity awareness training often becomes a compliance checkbox exercise rather than a vehicle to educate employees and users on the latest threats. And unfortunately, the threat landscape today is changing at a frenetic pace. Threat actors are taking advantage of AI tools and platforms to accelerate, enhance, and scale their attacks, whether it's social engineering schemes or wide-ranging supply chain compromises.

Thankfully, as the editors explain, some organizations are updating their programs to take more specific, line-of-business approaches for training while also accounting for the evolving threats related to AI; some programs are even using AI to create more convincing phishing simulations. Meanwhile, several US colleges and universities have increased their education offerings for AI security.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

The editors discuss these topics and more in this Reporters' Notebook episode.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright, senior news director at Dark Reading, and welcome to another edition of the Reporter's Notebook. I am here with Sharon and Eric. Would you guys like to introduce yourselves and then we'll get into the topics for today?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea: Hey, I am Sharon Shea. I'm the lead editor on Tech Target Cybersecurity.

Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller: And I'm Eric Geller. I'm a senior reporter at Cybersecurity Dive.

DR's Rob Wright: And this month is Cybersecurity Awareness Month. Yay! I know it's our favorite time of the year, right? We've written a fair amount of content on this topic over the last few weeks. We're still in it. We've still got about a week to go. It's not been a great run recently. There's been a lot going on, a lot of attacks, a lot of threats, a lot of urgent stuff going on in cybersecurity. But we wanted to get into some of those things here in this video discussion. Sharon, do you want to kick us off?

Related:Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

TTC's Sharon Shea: Yeah, so I will kind of take it back to the human side of Cybersecurity Awareness Month and then we can jump into some of the attack stuff later. But you know, one of the big things in Cybersecurity Awareness Month is making sure that your training programs are up to par. And granted, it's not just this month, just like Earth Day is not just one day for the Earth. We want it to be year-round.

But it does kind of give a springboard, as we called it in one of our articles, to further focus on cybersecurity throughout the year and bring a renewed focus for this month. And one report I was reading, a SANS report, said that 19% of organizations have cybersecurity awareness training programs designed primarily to meet a specific compliance or audit requirement. And that's kind of a bad way to look at things, just doing this for compliance.

Obviously, you want to do it to be secure all the time. And, you know, we all probably groan when those awareness trainings come into our inboxes every couple months or a couple times a year. They can be boring and you just click through them just to get through them and do the checkbox. But sometimes those aren't quite as effective as they should be, as we've seen. Really, you don't want to treat it as a check space, compliance checkbox exercise.

Related:As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

And one major thing that we learned from our reporting, or I think we've known for years, but it's not one size fits all, right? You really want to identify the behaviors within your organization that create risk. You want to map those threats to business consequences, establish baselines, and monitor for deviations from those.

Threat s like deepfakes trying to get into your help desk and reset MFA or, you know, the common Arup example of the CFO who was on a call with an employee and wanted them to wire a ton of money to them. And you know, you really have to focus those down on what departments really need specific trainings. I guess within the organization, you have so many different types of people to cover. You have your general employees, you have C-level, privileged admins, HR recruiting, customer-facing employees, and you have third parties, contractors, and you want to match the awareness to those sorts of risks.

I guess another thing that we can talk about too is updating the program regularly. You do want to talk about older tech. We all know that phishing is a major thing, right? It's still a problem, but you also want to talk about the newer tech — AI. And not just AI — GenAI, agentic AI, you know, all these newest technologies from the past couple of years. People know how to securely use them as well as preventing their inherent security issues.

And another thing I thought was kind of cool that we've covered is using AI in your awareness programs. We were talking to one CISO who uses phishing — I'm sorry, uses phishing simulations created by AI to personalize them for their employees, which you know is pretty cool, too. It's not just that generic boring watching the same old video from, you know, the 1900s, probably.

TTC's Sharon Shea: Yeah. You know, so kind of to solve some of the problems too of those boring programs. One of our sources, Kevin Walker of Black Swan, told Alissa Irei that you know, you really want to do short training sprints versus real world marathons. Those hour-long trainings, no one's going to get them. You know, they're not gonna pay attention throughout this whole thing. So make them highly relevant, personalized, and you really want to have those short, easy-to-consume bits that are good for your employees.

I guess talking about specific threats towards specific employees, Rob, you had an example that you guys have been covering on Dark Reading lately.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, there's a lot going on lately with AI-themed attacks. And one of the things I've noticed — we covered this a couple, a few times actually — is that there's a lot of SEO poisoning and malvertising. I think we think of like malvertising and threats like that as kind of like low-hanging fruit, kind of the type of attacks that aren't very sophisticated and that don't go very far. Maybe you get like some malware on your system from a flash ad or like a comb-over ad or something like that.

And we're finding that these ads are getting a lot more — I hate using the word sophisticated, I hate it so much, it's so overused — they're getting more effective. There's not a lot of ad blockers that are going to get you around ads on Facebook and Meta, for example. And there was a recent report from Gen Digital — well, I think it was almost a year now — that they found that one out of every three ads on Instagram and Facebook was malicious. It either pointed to malware or some type of phishing link, or it was a scam, like an outright scam.

And what's happening these days is that attackers know that they can use sponsored links and they can use these types of ads, not just your conventional like pop-up ads and stuff like that, which a lot of people do block. But they can use those sponsored links, you can use Google ads, you can use really effective SEO poisoning techniques to put stuff out like, 'Hey, download Claude Code' or something like that, or like a new AI tool.

And there are so many people out there looking for these tools right now. There are so many people, there's so much shadow AI that it's just easy to come across one of these malicious links, whether you're actively looking for it or you're just playing around — who knows? And they're hosted on legitimate infrastructure, they're hosted on — there was a report recently that Any.Run had, there were some stats about how many attacks, AI-themed attacks, are being deployed and there was a report about just massive use of Cloudflare Pages as infrastructure so it looks legitimate and then there's also like OpenAI Custom GPTs and that like that just it just looks legitimate because it's on like a real provider like it's on OpenAI or it's on Cloudflare.

And it's very easy to get tripped up by these things and click on something and then immediately download an infostealer that gets your credentials. And if you're a developer, there's been so many attacks on developers. And it's just bad news for an organization. So I think one of the things that companies ought to focus on right now is just trying to get people within the organization — obviously it depends on like what your privilege level is and where you are in the organization — but really for any type of employee that's out there looking for an AI tool, you've got to know the risk. You have to know that a lot of the stuff that you're going to be digging up out there, if it's not through an official app store of for an official channel, it very well likely could be a scam or some type of social engineering scheme that's going to drop an infostealer or something worse on your system. So that was kind of an eye opener for us.

Scary stuff. And we're not even to Halloween, so we'll see. Eric, what have you been seeing?

CD's Eric Geller: Well, I looked at things from the perspective of the next generation workforce. We're talking a lot about educating the workforces of today and trying to mitigate the threats of today. But we're also seeing a lot of change in the AI landscape that it's been difficult for the current workforce to get their heads around. So I kind of focused on preparing the next workforce to understand not only AI, but also how to guard against threats related to AI.

So, how to be an AI security practitioner, how to focus on AI security governance and risk management. And I looked at the university level to understand what kinds of courses exist out there to prepare students for careers in this area. It's no surprise that there's a lot of AI curriculum at the higher education level. What might be more of a surprise is that universities have actually gotten pretty good over the past few years at recognizing that there needs to be a security component to that work.

So I spoke to people at a number of schools that have tried to build or begin building curricula around AI security. Spoke to folks at Carnegie Mellon. They have a certificate program in AI security that's designed for kind of mid-level corporate workers who want to specialize in this area to go in for a class. It's a few weeks, you come out with a certificate that can kind of prepare you to be a leader in this space. But of course, a lot of this is happening at the undergraduate and graduate level. And so there's a lot of courses designed to kind of grab folks at that point in their early, early pre-careers, if you will, and teach them why this is an important subject.

So I spoke to a professor at Georgia Tech who is teaching a graduate course in LLM security and said that she was actually surprised by how much interest there's been in AI security when she teaches you know, undergraduate level sort of cyber one one and she talks about large language models, there's a lot of interest in following up outside of class and trying to learn more about that specific part of cyber.

For those of us who are perhaps a little pessimistic that college students want to focus on security when all the money and the attention is in building and deploying new products, I think this story that I wrote was kind of a somewhat of a corrective to that narrative, but also just as a source of optimism that at least according to the folks who are teaching this material, there are folks interested in learning about this kind of stuff and there are folks interested in pursuing graduate school education and getting certificates specifically in the security part of AI, which again is good to see. And I think we're going to start to see a shift over the next few years as people come out of these programs and begin entering the workforce. We're going to see a more security minded attitude, I think, toward AI development, at least if some of these colleges get their way.

DR's Rob Wright: I'm actually, I suddenly have a positive outlook, which is really rare for me. I'm normally the pessimist.

DR's Rob Wright: Thank you. Yeah, no, that's great news. it sounds like a welcome development. So maybe there is something to look forward to with AI. Fingers crossed.

CD's Eric Geller: Yeah. And the one thing I'll add is that this is not just something that's siloed at specific universities. There are coalitions of schools working together to create curriculums, curricula that that they can you know use interchangeably, taking best practices that one school has found in terms of what works for teaching in the classroom, sharing that with other schools.

This is one area where the federal government is actually kind of playing a behind the scenes role because they sponsor this nationwide coalition that has sort of different schools have taken the lead on building their own little groups of schools that they work with to kind of create lesson plans, find subject matter that works in the classroom, and then share those lessons with each other. You know, academia is obviously a very collaborative sphere, and I think that works out to everyone's benefit here because the teachers that are finding things that work are are telling other teachers and other professors in other schools, you might want to try this approach. And there's a consortium that is kind of bringing all that together and trying to make this not necessarily the exact same curriculum at every school, but shared curricula across universities.

DR's Rob Wright: That's good. I'm optimistic, and I'm never optimistic. Well, thank you guys for coming together to discuss Cybersecurity Awareness Month and I'm glad we're ending it on a positive note. Thanks guys.

TTC's Sharon Shea: Thanks, Rob. Thanks, Eric.

#9946. Copilot Chat has usage caps, and Microsoft would rather you found them by hitting them

Mystery limits expand for users without the paid add-on, with upgrade prompts ready when features run dry

Microsoft is applying usage limits to more Copilot Chat features for commercial users without a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, and it won't publish the numerical caps.

Copilot Chat comes with qualifying Microsoft 365 business and enterprise subscriptions. Without the Copilot add-on, it can reason over web information and uploaded files. The paid license adds broader access to work data, including emails, meetings, chats, and documents.

Tasks already in progress won't be interrupted. Once a limit is reached, users will receive an in-product notice explaining when to retry the affected feature.

Administrators can't adjust these limits; Microsoft sets them. The Windows behemoth says it "doesn't publish specific limits because they're subject to change."

Microsoft also suggests that hitting a limit "might indicate interest in additional Copilot capabilities." The remedy it proposes for administrators to consider is, conveniently, another license.

Users may also be offered an upgrade route – although buying a license themselves depends on whether their organization permits self-service purchases. Microsoft explained: "In most organizations, the limit notification includes an option to upgrade.

"Users can select it to request a Microsoft 365 Copilot license from their admin, who can approve or deny requests in the Microsoft 365 admin center. If the organization allows users to buy licenses directly, users might also see an option to purchase a license."

Microsoft concluded: "Admins can turn off direct purchases for each product."

The rollout began on November 2 for organizations with 2,000 or fewer Microsoft 365 seats and is due to start on November 9 for larger organizations. It also applies only to users without a Microsoft 365 Copilot license in commercial tenants. Web, desktop, and mobile apps are all affected.

The change could be Microsoft's latest wheeze to turn included Copilot Chat access into paid add-on sales. Users who hit an unpublished ceiling may well start pestering administrators for an upgrade.

The alternative is that admins decide tighter controls are preferable to unpredictable feature availability. Not necessarily the sales outcome Microsoft had in mind. ®

#9945. Run a vLLM Server on HF Jobs in One Command

You can spin up a private, OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint on Hugging Face infrastructure with a single command — no servers to provision, no Kubernetes, pay-per-second. Once it's up, you can query it from your laptop, a notebook, or anywhere else.

It's the quickest way to stand up a model for tests, evals, or batch generation. (If you're after a managed, production-ready service instead, that's what Inference Endpoints are for — more on when to pick which at the end.)

hf jobs run is docker run for HF infrastructure. We use the official vllm/vllm-openai image, ask for a GPU with --flavor, and expose vLLM's port with --expose:

--expose 8000 routes the container's port through HF's public jobs proxy (see the Serve Models guide for the full reference). The command prints the URL your server is reachable at:

6a381ca1953ed90bfb947332 is your job ID. Keep track of it, we'll need it. We'll use as a placeholder for it in the rest of the post.

Give it a couple of minutes to download weights and boot. When the logs show Application startup complete, you're live.

vLLM speaks the OpenAI API, and every request just needs your HF token as a bearer token. The quickest way to hit it is curl:

which returns the usual OpenAI-style JSON, with choices[0].message.content holding "Hello! How can I assist you today? 😊".

Or, from Python, point the OpenAI client at the exposed URL and pass the token as the API key:

Quick health check before you start: curl https://--8000.hf.jobs/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer $(hf auth token)" should list the model.

🔐 The endpoint is gated, not public. Every request must carry an HF token with read access to the job's namespace. A plain browser visit will be rejected. In effect, the jobs proxy is your API gate: access is scoped to you (and your org). That's fine for private use, but treat the URL accordingly: don't share it expecting it to be open, and don't paste your token into untrusted places. If you need finer-grained or public access, put a proper gateway in front instead. Or see HF Jobs or Inference Endpoints? below.

Jobs are billed per second, so stop the server when you're done:

The --timeout you set is a safety net (it'll auto-stop), but cancelling explicitly is cheaper. An a10g-large runs at $1.50/hour — check hf jobs hardware for the full price list and pick the smallest flavor that fits your model.

The same command scales to much larger models — pick a beefier --flavor and tell vLLM to shard the model across the GPUs with --tensor-parallel-size. For example, the 122B Qwen3.5 mixture-of-experts model on 2× H200:

--tensor-parallel-size should match the number of GPUs in the flavor (h200x2 → 2, h200x8 → 8). Run hf jobs hardware to see what's available and give bigger models a longer --timeout, since they take longer to download and load. For large models, H200 flavors are usually the best value.

The --max-model-len 32768 --max-num-seqs 256 flags are specific to this model: Qwen3.5-122B is a hybrid Mamba/attention architecture with a 256K-token default context, which doesn't leave enough memory for vLLM's default batch settings. Capping the context length and concurrent-sequence count keeps it within the GPUs' memory. If a model fails to start with an out-of-memory or cache-block error, dialing these two down is the first thing to try. Everything else (the exposed URL, the OpenAI client, the token auth) stays exactly the same.

Prefer a chat window over curl? A few lines of Gradio point at the same endpoint. Add --reasoning-parser deepseek_r1 to the vllm serve command so Qwen3's thinking comes back as a separate field (not necessary, but helpful), then run this code locally (you'll just need the job ID):

Run it, open http://127.0.0.1:7860, and chat — reasoning streams into the collapsible panel, the answer below.

Need to debug a startup failure, watch GPU memory, or tail logs interactively? You can open a shell straight into the running job. Launch it with --ssh and make sure your public key is registered at huggingface.co/settings/keys:

You're now inside the container, where you can run nvidia-smi, inspect the process, or poke at the model directly — which makes debugging and monitoring much easier than reading logs from the outside. SSH support requires huggingface_hub >= 1.20.0.

The same endpoint can back a terminal coding agent. Pi is a provider-agnostic agent harness. Point it at the job and you get a Read/Write/Edit/Bash agent running on your own self-hosted model.

One thing to set up first: agents drive the model through tool calls, and vLLM only accepts those if the server is launched with tool calling enabled. So relaunch with --enable-auto-tool-choice and a --tool-call-parser matching the model family (hermes for Qwen3). Agents also benefit from a stronger model, so this is a good place to bring in the bigger one:

Then add the job as a custom provider in ~/.pi/agent/models.json:

The model you spun up a couple of commands ago, now driving an interactive coding agent in your terminal.

HF Jobs isn't the only way to serve a model on Hugging Face. Inference Endpoints are our managed product for the same job, and which one fits depends on what you're after.

Reach for HF Jobs when you want maximum flexibility and control: it's just docker run on HF infrastructure, so you pick the image, the exact vllm serve flags, and the hardware, and you pay per second for as long as the job runs. That makes it a great fit for experiments, one-off evals, batch generation, or kicking the tires on a model before committing to anything.

Reach for Inference Endpoints when you want something more production-ready. They add the operational niceties a long-lived service needs: finer-grained access control (an endpoint can be public, protected, or private), and scale-to-zero, so you're not billed during periods of inactivity. If you're standing up a durable endpoint rather than running a job, that's the tool to grab.

This post sticks to vLLM, but the same expose-a-port pattern works with any OpenAI-compatible server. To serve GGUFs with llama.cpp or run SGLang instead, see the Serve Models on Jobs guide, which walks through those backends.

#9944. DiScoFormer: One transformer for density and score, across distributions

Many problems in machine learning and the sciences come down to the same task: you have a collection of data points and want to recover the distribution they came from—which values are common, and which are rare. Pinning down that distribution means estimating two quantities: the distribution's density and, more useful as dimensionality grows, its score. The density is the smooth version of a histogram—high where points cluster and low where they're scarce. The score—the gradient of the log-density—points in the direction the density rises fastest: move a point along the score and it heads toward a more probable region.

Diffusion-based generative models (the technology behind AI image generators like Stable Diffusion and DALL-E) start from random noise and repeatedly follow the score, turning that noise into a realistic image. The same score drives Bayesian sampling and the particle simulations used to model systems such as plasma.

Extracting the density and score from a finite sample is challenging, and today's tools force a trade-off between generalizability and accuracy. One classical approach, kernel density estimation (KDE), computes the density at any location from the data points around it: the closer and more numerous they are, the higher the density. It needs no training and applies to any distribution, but its accuracy falls off sharply as dimensionality grows. Alternatively, neural score-matching models trained to predict the score stay accurate even in high dimensions, but each needs to learn the distribution and must be retrained from scratch for another.

We introduce a new solution called the DiScoFormer (Density and Score Transformer)—one model that, given a set of data points, estimates both the density and the score of the distribution in a single forward pass without retraining.

DiScoFormer maps an entire sample to the density and score of the distribution behind it using stacked layers of transformer blocks. The model utilizes cross-attention, which allows it to evaluate density and score at any point—not just where you have data. Score and density share a mathematical relationship: score is the gradient of the logarithm of density. We leverage this by having a shared backbone with two output heads, one for the density and one for the score.

This coupling does more than save parameters. The score head has to match the gradient of the log-density head at every query, so any gap between them is a label-free consistency loss. We use this at inference—hold the context fixed, take a few gradient steps on that consistency loss, and DiScoFormer adapts itself to an out-of-distribution input on the spot, no ground-truth density or score required.

There's a mathematical reason why the transformer architecture fits this task. Kernel density estimation has a single bandwidth—how far each point's influence reaches, fixed in advance and applied identically everywhere. Attention is a strict generalization of it: we analytically show that a single attention head's weights are nearly a Gaussian kernel over the data, so one cross-attention block can already reproduce KDE's density and score. From there the model goes further, learning several such scales at once and adapting them to the data. DiScoFormer doesn't discard the classical method for a black box but instead includes KDE as a special case and improves on it.

What data did we use to train DiScoFormer? We relied on Gaussian Mixture Models for two primary reasons. Firstly, GMMs are universal density approximators—with enough components they match essentially any smooth distribution to arbitrarily small error. Secondly, GMMs have closed-form densities and scores, so we always have an exact target to supervise against. We employ both of these properties by drawing a new GMM for every batch, giving the model virtually unlimited examples of target distributions and supervising each against a given GMM's exact density and score.

Across the board, DiScoFormer beats KDE at both density and score estimation, and the gap widens exactly where KDE struggles. In 100 dimensions, it isn't close—against the best hand-tuned KDE, it cuts score error by about 6.5x and density error by more than 37x, and it keeps improving as you add samples, while KDE runs out of memory. It also travels far outside its training data, staying accurate on mixtures with more modes than it ever saw during training and on non-Gaussian shapes like the Laplace and Student-t. KDE's main advantage remains speed, especially when datasets are small.

The part about DiScoFormer that we find most promising is that score estimation is a shared dependency across many fields, such as generative modeling, Bayesian inference, and scientific computing. A pretrained, plug-in estimator that stays accurate in high dimensions and removes the need to retrain per problem could cut that cost across all of them at once—one model, reused everywhere score and density show up.

We encourage you to read our technical report for more details.

#9943. OpenAI releases GPT-6 Cyber, and promises this one stays within 'rules of engagement'

The latest bug hunting model 'avoided exploiting out-of-scope services over 99 percent of the time', claims House of Altman

OpenAI, on Thursday, released its latest cybersecurity-tuned model, GPT-6 Cyber, which the House of Altman says combines "stronger cybersecurity capabilities with better adherence to researchers’ rules of engagement."

The new model, we’re told, is much better at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, compared to GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra.

OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra in early September, and less than a month later, killed off the planned release of GPT-6.1 Astra after the model got better at pursuing tasks but worse at staying within the boundaries of what it had actually been authorized to do.

The model maker said the latest cyber model was "trained to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions and report results accurately."

In OpenAI's ExploitGym training evaluation, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5 percent. For comparison, GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1 percent on these same benchmark tests.

"In a separate evaluation of whether the model respects the boundaries of an assigned task, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services over 99 percent of the time," Open AI said. Only 0.07 percent of cases went beyond the intended scope of the training exercise.

OpenAI declined to provide additional details about what happened in that 0.07 percent of cases and whether they involved any real-life safety or security incidents - like hacking companies or carrying out supply chain attacks as its earlier models have done during training. We do know, however, that OpenAI recently began denying internet access to the frontier models it is training to help prevent its models from doing bad things.

The latest cyber model is also really good at finding and exploiting serious security vulnerabilities, OpenAI claimed. Its researchers used GPT-6 Cyber to find 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, which Mozilla has started fixing. The model also helped researchers develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including 588 previously unknown bugs. The Linux findings are being reported with potential patches for maintainer review.

OpenAI classified GPT-6 Cyber as “Critical” under its Preparedness Framework. This is its highest-risk tier for cyber capabilities, and means a model can both identify and develop functional zero-day exploits in real-world critical systems, and execute end-to-end cyberattacks.

As such, it’s initially only available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers - these are customers who are authorized to use OpenAI’s models for offensive security actions such as proof-of-concept exploit development, exploit-chain validation, penetration testing, and red teaming.

Over the coming weeks, OpenAI will expand access to all Daybreak Red customers, and is also making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to this group, as well.

The model release comes as OpenAI makes a concerted push to improve the security of its products.

Earlier this week, OpenAI raised its bug bounty reward payments, and added new bonuses for independent researchers.

This includes quadrupling reward-range midpoints, on average, for medium, high and critical findings, so a critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000 - or up to or $51,577 after bonuses - compared to the previous $6,500 payout.

Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses.®
